#4314. Zelda: Ocarina of Time Review: A Modern Remake With an Old Soul

Nintendo brings one of gaming's most influential adventures into the modern era without losing the magic that made it special.

I don't think I'll ever forget the first time I played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Not because I remember every detail of that first adventure, but because it was literally the first video game I ever played.

I was just a little kid who barely understood English, sitting in front of a Nintendo 64 with a controller (which, yes, wasn't even connected to the console because I was the younger sister) and a dictionary by my side. I had no idea what half the characters were saying, but I knew I wanted to see what happened next. Nearly 30 years later, I find myself returning to that same adventure, this time with a much better understanding of English and a controller that actually works. And, surprisingly enough, I think this might be one of the most emotionally powerful experiences I've had with a remake in a long time.

From Darksiders to Shinobi: Art of Vengeance, I present to you ten action-adventure games that are unexpected masterpieces.

Sure, we all know how revolutionary Ocarina of Time was back in 1998. Its approach to 3D level design, exploration, combat, and storytelling helped shape the entire industry, establishing a reference that countless games would follow for decades. But this remake doesn't seem interested in proving that all over again.

So, rather than trying to reinvent one of gaming's most influential adventures, Nintendo seems much more interested in touching something deeper than any groundbreaking mechanic ever could: the memories we built with this little boy, his fairy, and a world that once felt impossibly big.

For starters, let's get one thing out of the way: despite Nintendo's pre-release marketing describing this as a ground-up remake a few times, don't expect something along the lines of Square Enix's Final Fantasy VII Remake trilogy. This is actually a faithful recreation of the original, much closer in spirit to what Nintendo did with Ocarina of Time and Majora's Mask on the Nintendo 3DS.

The main story remains practically untouched, the overall structure is familiar, and most of the changes come in the form of visual improvements, quality-of-life adjustments, and a handful of additions that make the experience feel more modern. This means that if you've played the original, you'll recognize almost everything here.

And I can understand that this might disappoint some people. When a remake is announced as being built from the ground up, it's natural to expect substantial changes, perhaps even a new interpretation of familiar locations, mechanics, or story moments. But I think it all comes down to what you expect from this particular adventure in the end.

If you've played the original, you'll recognize almost everything here.

As a longtime Zelda fan who literally learned how to play video games with Link, I found this approach much more effective than I initially imagined, since it allowed the remake to strike a point much deeper than any new fancy level design could ever reach, largely because it understands that Ocarina of Time doesn't need a completely different story to make us feel something all over again.

Instead, it gives us that very same story with a series of carefully considered tweaks. Some are immediately noticeable, while others are the kind of little details you might not even realize have changed until you've spent a few hours exploring Hyrule again. And there's no better place to start discussing these changes than with the story itself.

If you've somehow never experienced Ocarina of Time, here's the short version: you're a little boy without a fairy who happens to oversleep one morning, only to be awakened by a very concerned fairy named Navi. Before long, you're thrown into a journey to save the world, involving a mysterious princess and an evil Gerudo king.

It's a wonderfully straightforward premise that gradually evolves into something much bigger, exploring themes of childhood, growing up, loss, and how the passage of time feels bittersweet for us all. And, nearly three decades later, its emotional impact remains remarkably intact. However, the remake introduces something that makes these familiar moments feel considerably more powerful: dedicated cutscenes with voice acting.

The original Ocarina of Time did an incredible job with the hardware limitations of the Nintendo 64. Seriously, the developers managed to create some wonderfully expressive moments with not much to work with back then. But now, these scenes finally have the cinematic presentation they've always deserved – and boy, does it make a difference!

I honestly lost count of how many times I caught myself wearing the dumbest smile while watching a cutscene. Seeing Princess Ruto slowly abandon her grumpy attitude as she falls for Link, watching Darunia dance to Saria's Song as if he's attending the greatest concert of his life, or witnessing the moment we realize Ganondorf only managed to obtain the power he wanted because we essentially fell for his little scheme.

These scenes have so much more personality now, and the voice performances help give familiar characters a newfound sense of life. More importantly, they made me realize something rather unexpected: deep down, these were already the scenes I had imagined back in 1998. As a child, we had essentially created a full version of these moments in our heads, but the remake gave those childhood interpretations a proper visual and emotional form, and that's a pretty wonderful achievement!

More importantly, they made me realize something rather unexpected: deep down, these were already the scenes I had imagined back in 1998.

And speaking of giving familiar characters more room to breathe, there's another storytelling improvement here that I absolutely love: how NPCs are way more important now.

The remake's dev team included younger folks, several of whom never played the original Ocarina of Time, who provided a much-needed modern view of things.

One of my favorite things about Ocarina of Time has always been its worldbuilding. Hyrule is filled with strange, charming, and occasionally downright questionable people, each with their own little stories and quirks. But the remake takes this aspect of the original and expands it in a surprisingly meaningful way.

Here's a tiny detail that makes a huge difference around here: time now passes continuously within Hyrule's towns. Basically, in the original, the world essentially had four different environmental states: Child Link during the day and night, and Adult Link during the day and night. This allowed certain characters and events to appear depending on the time period and Link's age, but the system was somewhat restrictive because time wouldn't actually progress while you were exploring towns.

Now, the remake changes that! The sun rises and sets naturally as you explore even inside cities, with characters appearing and disappearing according to their own schedules (except in more contained areas such as temples and minigame shops).

It's a small adjustment that makes the towns feel much more organic, almost as if their inhabitants finally have their own agendas, which gives it a lovely Majora’s Mask vibe. Also, this adds additional events and dialogue associated with these new day-night cycles, giving us more opportunities to learn about people we previously knew very little about.

My favorite example of this is Grog, who is arguably one of the saddest characters in the entire game. Remember that punk-looking guy who sits beneath a tree in Kakariko Village at night, complaining that everyone he knows is disgusting? In the original, we only really encounter him twice: once as Child Link and later in the Lost Woods as Adult Link. Well, thanks to the new time system, you can now find him walking around Kakariko Village during the day, too. And he has more dialogue and new interactions, finally giving more weight to fan theories that have circulated about him for nearly 30 years!

And this isn’t an isolated example. Several other characters receive similar attention, making Hyrule feel like a much more interconnected place. I absolutely love this kind of addition because it doesn't just give us more content for the sake of having more content. It actually enriches a world we already know, rewards longtime fans who have spent years discussing its little mysteries, and makes its characters feel like actual inhabitants rather than people waiting for Link to show up. It just makes everything feel a little more real.

Okay, so the remake has the storytelling side covered. But what about the actual gameplay? After all, Ocarina of Time wouldn't have become such an influential title without its approach to exploration, combat, and puzzle-solving.

The good news is that the core experience remains remarkably faithful, although there are plenty of quality-of-life improvements that make returning to Hyrule considerably more comfortable.

For starters, the item menu has been reduced to three main tabs, with a much cleaner organization that makes finding and equipping things considerably easier. I have to admit that I wasn't particularly fond of the menu taking direct inspiration from Breath of the Wild, since different games have very different needs. However, the new quick-access carousel is an absolute lifesaver, and switching between items during exploration and combat feels much more fluid. You no longer have to spend quite so much time navigating menus just to equip something.

And there's also a second quick-access system dedicated to some of your most essential tools, including the Ocarina, Lens of Truth, Happy Mask Salesman's masks, and (yes, you can finally celebrate!) the Iron Boots. This last addition is particularly welcome because it addresses one of the most infamous frustrations of the original game: the Water Temple.

But don't think everything is perfect just because most changes are improvements. Some of the modernized design decisions have introduced a few restrictions that, to be completely honest, I'm not entirely convinced were necessary. For instance, certain pieces of equipment have been tweaked to prevent players from using them in ways the developers seemingly never intended.

This happened with the Hookshot, which was previously a wonderful tool for experimenting with different traversal possibilities, but now only attaches to specific designated surfaces. That means you can no longer use it to reach rooftops, for example. Does this force you to find alternative solutions? Sure. But it also takes away some of the creativity and freedom that made experimenting with the original game's mechanics so much fun.

Still, this is where expectations come into play again. And there is something important to highlight: overall, the remake makes your life considerably easier than it was back in 1998, which means that finding new solutions isn’t actually hard. Around here, NPCs offer more hints and several sequences have been optimized to deliver a more straightforward experience. Oh, and there's also a dedicated quest log that helps you keep track of both the main adventure and your secondary objectives.

While I wasn't particularly happy about the Hookshot changes, I never felt like they significantly compromised my experience. Finding alternative solutions was generally okay, and the improvements elsewhere made the overall gameplay feel much smoother. So it's a trade-off, and one that I think works more often than it doesn't.

Eiji Aonuma and the development team for the Ocarina of Time remake discussed how one of the original's infamous dungeons is being improved.

Now, here's where things get a little more complicated. As you might expect from a remake that's practically a 1:1 recreation, exploration remains very faithful to the original. And while the quality-of-life improvements make moving around Hyrule much more pleasant, they don't necessarily change how you interact with the world itself.

There are some additional visual indicators to help you find interesting things, though. Poes in Hyrule Field are now associated with specific fences, and Lake Hylia is no longer “separated” from the field, for example, making some environmental details easier to identify locations worth investigating. But the overall level design is pretty much what we experienced back in 1998, for better or worse.

And I have mixed feelings about that. On one hand, revisiting these locations with modernized controls and an entirely new visual presentation is an incredibly emotional experience. I genuinely enjoyed wandering around places I hadn't seen in years, recognizing familiar spots, and discovering little details that I had completely forgotten about. It's the kind of experience that makes you want to stop every few minutes just to appreciate how much care went into recreating this world.

On the other hand, I can't help wondering whether the developers could have gone a little further, especially since Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom have completely changed our expectations of what exploring Hyrule can mean, giving us approximately 984,396 things to discover while traveling from point A to point B. Compared to those experiences, Ocarina of Time's more structured approach can feel a little restrictive, particularly when you know exactly where everything is supposed to be.

I would have loved to see a few more surprises along the way, perhaps additional secrets or expanded areas that rewarded players for approaching familiar locations from a different perspective. But, once again, I need to consider what this remake is trying to accomplish. As someone with an almost unhealthy amount of nostalgia running through my veins, I honestly didn't mind revisiting a place I consider home, even if the journey remained largely unchanged! However, if you're expecting a completely redesigned Hyrule with new exploration mechanics and substantially expanded areas, I'd recommend keeping those expectations in check.

Now, let's talk about the elephant in the room: the visuals. The remake retains the colorful, whimsical identity of the original, but practically everything has been reimagined from an aesthetic standpoint. Hyrule now looks even more like a fantasy world, with lush environments, intricate textures, expressive character models, and an almost overwhelming amount of environmental detail.

I have to confess that the new art direction took some getting used to. Kokiri Forest, in particular, initially felt a little too dense for my taste. Come on, don't any of these Kokiri kids own a lawn mower? And Young Link's redesigned appearance also gave me some mixed feelings during my first few hours.

But the more I played, the more the new aesthetic grew on me. Before I knew it, I was completely obsessed with how beautiful everything looked. And a big part of that comes down to the character designs. Rather than simply updating existing models with higher-resolution textures, the developers have reimagined several characters and enemies to better fit the remake's more elaborate fantasy aesthetic. The result feels cohesive, and there's a clear sense of inspiration behind practically every design.

Not to mention the little details! You can see (and feel, since this game is all about feelings, right?) just how much attention went into recreating familiar locations. Kakariko Village's well, for example, now features carefully rendered water and a variety of textures that make the environment feel considerably more tangible. Even something as simple as watching Link play the Ocarina becomes a visual treat, since you can actually see his fingers moving to the correct notes.

Also, the developers clearly know which details longtime fans care about. One particularly memorable example is how they've handled one of the game's most terrifying creatures (you know who!), since it is scarier than ever. And several bosses have also received additional visual details and updated animations that make their encounters feel more imposing.

And it's these little touches that make the difference! The remake doesn't just want Hyrule to look prettier; it wants every familiar corner to feel worth revisiting. And, honestly, I could spend hours just walking around and appreciating it all.

Putting everything together, I think it's fair to say that this is a remake that successfully modernizes a classic without losing its old soul. And considering how heavily nostalgia has influenced the gaming industry lately, with remakes and remasters seemingly arriving every other month, it's nice to see one that understands exactly what made its source material so special.

Most of the improvements are welcome, even if a few decisions (sorry, I still won't forgive what happened to the Hookshot) leave something to be desired. The updated gameplay makes the experience feel much more accessible, the visual overhaul is gradually gorgeous, and the additional storytelling touches give familiar characters a newfound sense of personality.

Putting everything together, I think it's fair to say that this is a remake that successfully modernizes a classic without losing its old soul.

There are also several additions that I’m obsessed with, from hearing iconic characters speak for the first time to seeing long-standing fan theories receive more attention, not to mention the extra Ocarina mechanics that let you hum melodies into the microphone to play them. It's a collection of thoughtful changes that, when put together, makes this adventure feel surprisingly fresh without sacrificing what made it so memorable.

And that's precisely why I think this remake works so well for longtime fans. It doesn't ask us to forget the original or replace the memories we built with it. Instead, it gives us an opportunity to experience those same feelings again, now with a presentation and gameplay that feel right at home in 2026. But I also believe it works wonderfully as an entry point for newcomers! Despite its faithful structure, the modernized controls, expanded guidance, and quality-of-life improvements make the experience feel far less dated than the original. So you can still appreciate everything that made Ocarina of Time revolutionary without having to deal with every limitation of a game released nearly three decades ago.

In the end, this remake made me feel like that little kid again, waking up early on Saturday mornings to spend hours exploring Hyrule, controller in hand (and, thankfully, connected this time). And I could feel that this was exactly what Nintendo wanted to accomplish within the first few minutes.

Playing this remake reminded me that video games can be much more than the mechanics we praise, the level design we analyze, the technical achievements we celebrate, or framerates that we fear to drop. Sometimes, their greatest power lies in how they make us feel, even decades after we've first experienced them – and Ocarina of Time still has that magic. Now, if you'll excuse me, I still have a few Golden Skulltulas and Heart Pieces to collect. And then? Well, I think I'm ready for another adventure.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is one of the most beloved games of all time, but these remakes might be just as meaningful to fans.

#4313. Love and Deepspace 5.0 update brings together all five love interests for the first time

Love and Deepspace is getting a big update to celebrate its second anniversary, and there's a lot to dig through.

If you can believe it, Love and Deepspace is almost two-years-old, and Infold Games is celebrating the moment in a few major ways. The Throne of Eros update brings the game up to version 5.0, and it’s one for fans of all love interests.

For one, this is the first time all five of them are brought together. The update is also adding some important new features, alongside anniversary events, and more.

Throne of Eros also doubles as the new Wish Pool, which is the one that has all of the game’s love interests in a single banner. This is a limited-time affair, of course, but it’s not the only thing you should look forward to here.

There’s also the Memory Growth Bonus, another limited-time event that you can take advantage of to grow your Memories. The even bigger news is that you can target your Wishes through the Xspace Echo, which lets you select five Memories to create your own pool from. You can use this to get any Memories you might not have, of course.

On the topic of Memories, you’ll also be able to unlock new second anniversary KV Memories, as part of a Yearly Highlights Event that will let you look back on your own journey with the game over the past year.

On the story and narrative side, Throne of Eros adds two new main stories, with new branches for Xavier, and Rafayel. There’s even a narrative-specific event that will run throughout the anniversary period, through which you can earn two daily outfits for each of the five love interests.

The celebrations also extend to new anniversary content like mail, and video calls. You can purchase a Yearly Pass, and check out some new arrivals at the Lunar Shop.

Beyond the anniversary content, version 5.0 also adds a new feature to the game: Home, which essentially offers a hub to get you directly to interacting with love interests that doesn’t have to do with combat or story.

You can also expect various other quality of life updates that touch on the Journal, Phone Moments Search, Resources Quick Cleanup, and new Tete-a-Tete that should make interacting with all of them more streamlined.

#4312. KRÜ Blaze recover from opening map loss to beat Shopify Rebellion Gold and reach final

KRÜ Blaze dropped the first map and then took the next three on Saturday 31 October. The win reverses their upper bracket semi-final defeat to Shopify Rebellion Gold and sends the Argentine-based side into the final of the VCT Game Changers Championship 2026. Shopify Rebellion Gold’s campaign ends with the loss.

The result also cuts against the power rankings. Shopify Rebellion Gold arrived as the 10th-ranked team with a rating of 1782. KRÜ Blaze sit 20th on 1742, although their 63-21 record across 84 rated matches is the stronger of the two.

Shopify Rebellion Gold struck first, taking a 47-minute opening map. KRÜ Blaze levelled on the quickest map of the series, which lasted 37 minutes, and edged ahead with a 50-minute third.

The fourth map was by some distance the longest of the night at 70 minutes. KRÜ Blaze closed it out to settle the best-of-five without needing a decider.

The meeting on 27 October had been far more one-sided. Shopify Rebellion Gold won that upper bracket semi-final 2-0, which pushed KRÜ Blaze into the lower half of the draw. Before that, KRÜ Blaze had opened their playoff run by beating Gen.G GC 2-1 in the upper bracket quarter-finals.

Saturday’s victory was KRÜ Blaze’s third successive series win in the lower bracket. Both earlier wins were sweeps. They beat Team Liquid Brazil 2-0 in the quarter-finals, then dispatched MIBR GC by the same score in the semi-finals.

That run means they have won seven of the eight maps played since dropping out of the upper bracket. They also came into the event as winners of the Latin America regional final, where they beat Akave Esports Black 3-1.

#4310. Genshin Impact Version Luna 4 introduces three new playable characters, including the long-awaited Moon Maiden Columbina

The first major Genshin Impact update in 2026 is almost here, bringing characters we've been waiting a while to play, and more besides.

Genshin Impact’s latest Special Program has spilled all the beans on the game’s next major update, Luna 4. The update, which arrives on January 14, kicks off 2026 with several bits of new content, including some previously-teased characters.

Dubbed Traveler on a Winter's Night, Luna 4 introduces three new playable characters, and brings back The Lantern Rite event to celebrate the beginning of the new year.

The first new arrival in Version Luna 4 is Columbina Hyposelenia, the Moon Maiden. Columbina is a 5-Star Hydro Catalyst wielder. Her kit revolves around supporting the squad via Lunar Reactions. She can trigger coordinated Lunar Reaction DMG, even when she’s off the field.

The Moon Maiden’s special ability, Lunar Domain, further boosts all Lunar Reactions by applying a DMG bonus, including summoning more thundercloud strikes for Lunar-Charged reactions. Columbina is also capable of converting Electro-Charged, Bloom, and Hydro Crystallize reactions into Lunar Reactions, as well as revive fallen squad members.

Speaking of elemental reactions, new in this version is Lunar-Crystallize, a new reaction that’s triggered when Geo meets Hydro (under certain conditions). When triggered, Lunar-Crystallize summons three Moondrifts near enemies. When triggered three times, Moondrift Harmony gets activated, dealing Geo DMG to enemies caught in its radius.

Then there’s Zibai, an Adeptus from Liyue. Zibai is another 5-Star character, a Geo Sword wielder. Zibai can, through entering a special state where they can build up energy, unleash an Elemental Skill that deals Lunar-Crystallize DMG.

The longer the fight goes on, the more Lunar-Crystallize reactions are triggered, the higher (and more often) the damage of Zibai’s Elemental Skill becomes.

Luna 4 continues the Nod-Krai story arc, with a big confrontation with Il Dottore. This is the focus of the new Archon Quest, completing which will earn you a new outfit. There’s a gameplay element to that new chapter, too, with the reveal of Piramida, a new area north of the region. Piramida is the headquarters of the Lightkeepers.

The first phase of Luna 4’s Event Wishes will, unsurprisingly, feature Columbina. It’ll also include reruns of Ineffa. The second phase is when Zibai becomes available, alongside another newcomer: Illuga, a 4-Star, polearm-wielding Geo Lightkeeper. The second phase’s rerun will be Neuvillette, who’s also going to have a new outfit in the shop at a discount.

Version Luna 4 brings back the annual Lantern Rite event, taking place in the mainland of Liyue. The event features its own set of minigames with unique rewards, alongside new stories of the Adepti.

All around Liyue Harbor, you’ll be able to place Xiao Lanterns and inscribe them with messages for others to read. You’ll also earn some Fortune Coins from Auspicious Treasure Trees, which you can later exchange for gifts.

All players will receive 1,600 Primogems through the in-game mail. If you log in regularly, you can earn up to ten Intertwined Fates. Lantern Rite has a new outfit for Yaoyao, which is also where you have a chance to earn one 4-Star Liyue character for free.

Finally, you can look forward to the new Classic Mode in Miliastra Wonderland, which lets you invite select Teyvat characters to join you.

#4307. d4v41 and Jinggg leave Paper Rex after 7th–8th Champions finish, Pacific place secure

Paper Rex has parted with captain d4v41 and Jinggg, two Masters Toronto winners, after an early exit at Champions 2026. With its VCT Pacific partner place secure, the Singapore organisation is rebuilding by choice as free agency opens to every region.

Paper Rex has broken up the core of its VALORANT roster. The Singapore organisation is parting with its captain and one of its best-known players as the 2027 season approaches. d4v41 had been with Paper Rex since its founding in 2020. He played first on its CS:GO roster, then moved with the team to VALORANT. Jinggg joined on 28 September 2021.

Neither player has named a destination. In the farewell video Paper Rex released, d4v41 said he was moving to a new team. Jinggg wrote on X that he was excited about what comes next. d4v41 also asked fans to keep supporting the organisation after both have gone.

The split follows a season that faded at the end. Paper Rex were runners-up at both Masters Santiago and Masters London earlier in 2026. At Champions in Shanghai, they lost 2-0 to LOUD in the upper-bracket quarter-finals on 7 October. A 2-1 defeat to T1 in lower-bracket round one ended their run on 9 October. The event carried a $2,250,000 prize pool. LOUD went on to beat Team Vitality in the final.

The pair leave with a long record together. Jinggg helped Paper Rex to second place at Masters Copenhagen 2022. He was also part of the run to the Champions 2023 final, where the team were runners-up. Liquipedia lists both players in the line-up that won VCT 2025 Masters Toronto.

The changes are not forced by the league. The organisation is owned by IMPLS Entertainment Pte Ltd. Riot has cut the number of partner teams in each region from ten to eight for 2027–28. That leaves 32 across the four regions.

The Pacific format rewards that security. The eight partners receive seeded places at Kickoff in January 2027. Four further places go to teams that come through open qualifiers. Paper Rex can therefore reshape its roster without needing to qualify.

Two Masters winners on the open market could matter well beyond the Pacific. EMEA’s eight partners for 2027 are Fnatic, BBL Esports, FUT Esports, Team Heretics, Team Liquid, Gentle Mates, Karmine Corp and Team Vitality. Under Riot’s open qualifier rules, most regions require three of a team’s five players to come from that region. Teams must also keep three of five players between events to carry their progress forward. Those limits will frame how far any club can rebuild around new signings.

Khalish has been part of Paper Rex since our founding in 2020, starting first on our CS:GO Roster and transitioning with the team to VALORANT. We'll always remember the laughs, the op shots, and every achievement through the years.

From everyone at Paper Rex, we wish @d4v41vlr… pic.twitter.com/UgWKD4QfOj

Later in November, open qualifiers get under way. The season’s first Masters event follows in February 2027.

#4303. Diablo 4's long-awaited Tower and its Leaderboards enter beta today, and there's no PTR funny business this time

Diablo 4's first big moment of 2026 is nearly upon us, and it's one feature many have been looking forward to for actual years.

Diablo 4 is about to deliver on Blizzard’s years-old promise to add a challenging, leaderboard-driven experience to the action RPG. The beta for The Tower, and its associated Leaderboards are about to kick off.

As recently revealed, the new experience launches today at 11am PT, 2pm ET, 7pm GMT. This is a beta version that arrives alongside update 2.5.2.

This early launch won’t offer the full experience, and it’s mainly designed to get it into the hands of players early so that Blizzard could get as much feedback as possible and incorporate it into the final version.

The beta is available to everyone, which is a nice change from the usual rigmarole players would have to go through to get the PTR build and play on a different branch. The Tower, and Leaderboards will be available only in the Seasonal Realm, however. Indeed, the plan is to build on what’s there with each future season, so it’s best to think of it as a seasonal experience.

The Tower is about as simple of an activity as you can get in an action RPG. The goal is to climb as many floors as you can as quickly as you can, all while battling increasingly difficult mobs.

You need to reach and beat the Tower’s final boss before you can call it a run. The Leaderboard will then show your time, and let you see how well you did compared to other players.

The Tower is available to anyone who completed Rank 2 of the current Season Rank. Once done, an Obelisk will appear in Cerrigar, letting you access the challenge.

The Leaderboards themselves will operate on a two-week schedule, all of which will take place during a given season. In this case, they’re going to close the day before Season of the Divine Interversion - the game’s current season - ends.

Blizzard published an updated set of patch notes that show how much has changed since The Tower, and Leaderboards first became playable in the patch 2.5.0 PTR.

Though the two new additions have been anticipated for a while, there’s not been much exciting going on in the world of Diablo 4, apart, of course, from the surprise arrival of The Paladin class, which became available in December last year to coincide with the announcement of Lord of Hatred, the game’s next expansion.

#4300. The Sims developer vows "our values are unchanged," as it teases multiple projects from post-Saudi-owned EA

The team behind one of EA's most diverse franchises has issued a statement about its future under the soon-to-be Saudi-owned publisher.

In their (slightly belated) new years message to players, the developer of EA’s The Sims series of games has lightly addressed concerns about its future within the publisher in a wide-ranging letter to the community.

The letter also serves as something of a light plan for what players can expect soon, and in the future, alongside what the various teams are currently working on.

The developer starts off the yearly check-in with a statement that attempts to address concerns about the future of The Sims, historically one of EA’s most inclusive and culturally diverse franchises.

This, of course, comes in the wake of last year’s bombshell that EA is being taken private by a coalition led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), alongside investment firms Silver Lake Capital and Affinity Partners. The $55 billion acquisition was approved by EA’s shareholders in December, and is set to close by the end of June.

Understandably, many raised concerns about what EA’s new ownership would mean for its people, and portfolio of games. The news is concerning for The Sims in particular, a series that’s long embraced diversity and inclusivity, and has historically been popular among women, people of colour, and members of the LGBTQ+ community.

“Our Sims team's creative control, guided by our values of inclusivity, choice, creativity, community, and play, has not changed,” the post reads, though without referring to the buyout directly at any point.

“These values inspire the decisions we make each and every day as we plan for today, tomorrow, and the future.”

As for what’s to come in 2026 and beyond, it sounds like The Sims team has multiple irons in the fire. The developer is working on “a family of new Sims experiences” that will find homes on PC, console, and mobile. Crucially, the post says that not every experience will be on every platform, in order for each to focus on delivering something different and interesting.

Future releases, of course, include new The Sims 4 content that focuses on the single-player experience. The social and more multiplayer-driven experiences, however, will instead be found in Project Rene, the mobile-first life-sim currently in development. (Despite early confidence that it was a working title for The Sims 5, it's now confirmed that Project Rene won’t, in fact, be a direct successor to The Sims 4.)

Some of these projects will see more playtesting throughout 2026, so you should probably sign up for The Sims Labs if you want to hear about when/how you can get involved.

#4299. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Goes Nuclear Against ‘Lobby Shopping’

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

Players have used third-party applications to assist their play for years now, to mixed success and intent. Many benign apps for games like League and Valorant give easier access to community info, while other, more malicious cheats can completely ruin a game for everyone else in the lobby.

After unjustly banning a Battlefield 6 player, EA lost a court case to keep the ban in place.

Call of Duty: Warzone players have been utilizing one of the oddest forms of cheating I’ve ever heard of, peeking at the skill level of everyone in the lobby through the app Warzone Agent to decide whether or not to just leave the game. Activision has announced they’re clamping down hard on the practice, looking to eliminate it going forward.

Call of Duty players have been complaining about the franchise’s skill-based matchmaking (SBMM) for years now, a system where players are matched against foes equivalent to their skill level. This is, of course, how most matchmaking systems work, but COD players have been asking for its elimination since the original Modern Warfare remake.

In order to avoid these close matches, they utilize apps like Warzone Agent to figure out the average rank of the lobby before deciding to play, a practice Warzone’s anti-cheat division, Ricochet, has officially stood against. In their release surrounding the practice of lobby shopping, “moving forward, players who leave Warzone Agent loaded will not be able to access Multiplayer modes.”

Lobby shopping is the practice of hopping around warm-up stage lobbies to search for one with a lower skill ceiling, essentially targeting worse players to maximize your own boons. Activision has made it clear they won’t stand to suffer the practice any longer, further saying, “using unauthorized software to manipulate the player experience violates Activision Terms of Use and leaves your account and hardware subject to enforcement.”

Many benign apps for games like League and Valorant give easier access to community info, while other, more malicious cheats can completely ruin a game for everyone else in the lobby.

Threatening to drop the ban hammer on violators is a great way to shake the practice off, and Activision isn’t stopping there, clarifying what it considers cheating. That includes external account boosting, led by swarms of bots they’ve managed to start stomping out.

Bots plague any free-to-play game people want to put time into, and focusing more on curtailing them is a great step toward slowing the flow, even if it is just a bandage over the wound. For now, Activision has drawn their line in the sand. The only question is whether or not they’ll flinch in the face of community complaints, but they’ve stuck by their guns this long.

The community complaint around skill-based matchmaking has always struck me as incredibly odd, with these players mostly desiring a true random selection process. These random matches are, on paper, more varied, but in practice lead to matches that are total stomps for one side or the other, leaving plenty of players with a bad taste in their mouths.

Getting to be the one stomping can be great fun, but that’s also possible against players of your skill level. SBMM’s main purpose is to minimize the games that feel like complete wipes from the loser’s perspective, keeping them playing against those who are actually equivalent to them on a broad scale. It’s far from perfect, but it's better than literally just tossing a random selection of players in a room.

Without it, not only would many casual players have to gamble on getting crushed every other game, but Activision could lose those players after enough rough matches, the true reason for the practice’s continued support. Despite the complaints, Activision has clearly long since decided that skill-based matchmaking is the best middle ground for skilled and casual players alike, giving everyone designated lobbies where they’re at least promised matches that are competitive.

Modern Warfare 4's launch party is still going, with a free play period for DMZ ready to rake in new players.

#4297. Here's The Best Graphics And Performance Mode For Phantom Blade Zero On PlayStation 5

Phantom Blade Zero is out now for everyone as a console exclusive on PlayStation 5 and on PC via Steam and the Epic Games Store as well. If you missed it, it's my favorite action game of the year so far, and you can read why in Game Informer's Phantom Blade Zero review. That explains why I think you should check the game out; Game Informer's list of Phantom Blade Zero tips and tricks will get you some key information I wish I had when I started the game; and this guide I wrote up about the requirements you need to get the best ending in Phantom Blade Zero will help you find all story-critical content in the game.

However, you're looking for advice on which of the three visual modes Phantom Blade Zero offers you should use on your PS5. This here piece is for you.

Phantom Blade Zero has three visual modes on PS5 Pro: Quality, Balanced, and Performance. I tested all three. My personal favorite was Balanced, which gives you an upscaled (checkerboarded) 4K resolution at 40 FPS, as long as you have a 120Hz TV with VRR. If you have a 120Hz TV, it likely has VRR because most major manufacturers include it with 120Hz. I like this mode because the upscaled 4K looks beautiful, just a hair less than native 4K, and if you aren't someone super trained on those details, I'd wager you won't notice the difference. The best part is that this mode offers 40 FPS gameplay, which, contrary to how math works, is halfway between 30 FPS and 60 FPS; I'm not kidding, look it up. As such, 40 FPS feels much smoother than 30 FPS, and you're still getting crisp 4K resolution. It's a win-win for me and my go-to mode when a game offers it. That said, if you don’t have a PS5 Pro, you won’t see this Balanced mode.

The Performance mode offers an upscaled 2K resolution with a pretty locked 60 FPS. Phantom Blade Zero is an extremely fast, fluid action game, so I think many people will want the buttery smoothness of 60 FPS gameplay. If that's you, pick the Performance mode. Sure, its resolution is lower, and it will look blurrier and less crisp than the other two modes, but if you aren't switching back and forth often or looking at side-by-side images, you likely won't notice.

Quality mode is native 4K resolution (absolutely beautiful, the best visual image you can get playing Phantom Blade Zero), but at 30 FPS... and for a game like this, I don't think 30 FPS does it justice. I don't really recommend this mode for combat, but if you're just waltzing around Wulin, grabbing screenshots and such, turn it on and bask in the wonders of developer S-Game's art team. Note: There is an option for ray tracing on PS5 Pro. I tested all three graphics modes with it on and off and noticed zero performance changes or issues. So, use ray tracing – it’s nice!

#4295. Jordan Esports Federation signs MoU with King Hussein Business Park to host more events

Priya Venkatesh has been following the money in esports since before brand deals were considered legitimate marketing. She got pulled into the scene through competitive fighting games and eventually found herself more interested in the contracts and partnerships behind the tournaments than the matches themselves. These days she focuses on how brands navigate esports sponsorships, where the smart money is going, and which deals are actually built to last versus the ones that look good in a press release.

The Jordan Esports Federation (JEF) has signed a memorandum of understanding with King Hussein Business Park (KHBP) in Amman, giving the national body a formal framework to stage more tournaments and events at the site it already calls home.

KHBP announced the deal on Sunday in a statement published on its website. Prince Omar bin Faisal, who is President of the JEF, attended the signing.

Under the MoU, the federation and the business park will jointly host and organise specialised competitions on the KHBP campus. They will also receive the international delegations and official guests that travel to those events. Beyond the competitive side, the two organisations plan to cooperate on media and marketing, look at shared education, training and community projects, and swap knowledge and expertise.

Neither party has disclosed financial terms or the length of the agreement.

KHBP CEO Eng. Ammar Ezzeddin presented the MoU as part of the park’s wider ambitions. “This partnership builds on our ongoing efforts to create an enabling environment for institutions, initiatives and high-potential sectors, and to establish KHBP as a hub for innovation and technology,” he said.

He added: “We look forward to helping the sector thrive and to hosting more tournaments and events that put Jordanian talent in the spotlight and raise the Kingdom’s profile in this field.”

JEF Vice President Hazem Bawab focused on the competitive and grassroots goals. “This partnership is a significant step in our drive to develop the esports industry in Jordan and elevate the standard of local, regional and international competitions and activities,” he said.

Bawab continued: “We look forward to drawing on the setup and capabilities that KHBP offers to scale our work, nurture young talent and launch joint programmes that help the industry grow and encourage greater participation.”

The deal formalises a relationship that already exists on the ground. According to The Esports Radar, the JEF, which is the government recognised regulator for esports in the country, is based at the park in West Amman.

A lot of that work happens at THE ARC, the arena and gaming dome inside the park. The same report lists past events there including the fourth Arab Esports League, a Women’s Esports Championship and Red Bull Login, which doubled as Jordan’s national final stage in Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2. The venue is also an incubation centre supported by the federation and the Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship, and runs training camps for players hoping to turn professional.

KHBP has been a destination for esports investment for some time. In 2024, lounge operator True Gamers announced plans for an esports venue in Jordan at the business park, a project in which its CPO publicly thanked the JEF and Prince Omar.

The timing also puts Amman in the industry spotlight. PocketGamer.biz points out that Pocket Gamer Connects Jordan takes place on 7 and 8 November, bringing many of the region’s games industry stakeholders to the city later this week.

My Hero Academia is a series that has rightfully garnered legions of fans, and even with the series having wrapped up, it remains immensely popular. But even I was surprised to find out that My Hero Ultra Rumble, the battle royale brawler, is set to make its way to mobile, with pre-registration now open!

My Hero Ultra Rumble is a 24-player battle royale that sees each match split into eight teams of three; from there, you take on the roles of your favourite characters, with their own distinctive quirks (the series' name for superpowers) used to ensure you're the last team standing.

Along the way, you can collect upgrades to enhance your abilities, and either threaten or rescue civilians caught in the crossfire depending on whether you're a hero or villain.

At the same time, it must be popular enough despite how often the community grouses about issues such as power creep. And while we don't have an official launch date yet, there's already plenty of pre-registration rewards available for early birds.

We'll just have to watch this space, I suppose. With many of you likely having played My Hero Academia's other mobile spinoffs, like My Hero Academia United Survival, I've no doubt there's plenty of Shonen fans chomping at the bit to give Ultra Rumble a go!

And in the meantime, if you want to see what other big mobile hits have been inspired by Japan's most famous cultural export, why not check out our list of the best anime games on mobile for some choice picks?

#4293. Battlefield 6 Season 2 delayed like many of us expected, but we're getting a new update and a bonus battle pass path

Battlefield 6 has pushed back its next season by nearly a month in order to refine Season 2 content and implement more of players' feedback.

Battlefield Studios has released its first official communication in 2026. Rather than unveil the second season of Battlefield 6, however, the developer instead announced a delay. The currently ongoing Season 1 was initially meant to end on Tuesday, January 20, hence why the developer had to communicate something this week.

Season 1 will now end on Tuesday, February 17, which is also when Season 2 will kick off. Given the current sentiment around the game, this news isn’t surprising in the least.

In the blog post announcing the delay, BF Studios said that the decision to extend the current season and push back the start of the next one allows for extra time to “further polish and refine” Season 2 content.

The developer did not offer any hints about Season 2, but there’s an incredibly brief teaser trailer featuring a soldier wearing a gas mask emerging from an environment drenched in toxic gas.

Given that Battlefield 6’s battle royale mode Redsec does not utilise the popular encroaching gas mechanic (using an encroaching ring of fire instead), it’s possible that we may be looking at something new in multiplayer akin to Battlefield 1. Of course, this may just be a visual piece that doesn’t reflect the gameplay of Season 2.

Escalating the fight with new threats on the battlefield.Season 2 begins February 17. pic.twitter.com/fGMegJJuTj

What we are getting news of today, however, is the game’s next patch. This extension update is going to arrive next week, on January 20, when Season 1 was supposed to end. It’s bringing new weekly challenges to the game, but its biggest addition is yet another Bonus Path to the battle pass. You can also expect the free daily login rewards to continue, alongside other periods of double XP.

Similar to other Bonus Paths, the new Frostfire Bonus Path can be completed alongside the Season 1 battle pass. You’ll need 110 Bonus Path Points in total if you want to earn everything it has to offer, with each tier requiring 10 points. It is worth noting, however, that Frostfire Points are only earned through weekly challenges, meaning there won’t be any bonus challenges associated with it.

Frostfire includes several new customisation rewards, of course, such as a Weapon Package, soldier skin, XP boosts and the usual run of unlocks.

Though the latest blog post may be devoid of any real details on Season 2, BF Studios confirmed that Battlefield Labs will play a larger role in offering a preview of what’s to come, so it’s entirely possible that the testing initiative will soon open its doors to players with an early look at some of the maps and other content planned for Season 2.

#4291. KRÜ Blaze win Game Changers Championship from lower bracket, ending Gentle Mates’ unbeaten run

KRÜ Blaze came through the lower bracket to beat Europe's Gentle Mates GC over five maps in São Paulo, giving LATAM its first Game Changers Championship title. They are also the last winners of the standalone event, as next year's final moves to Champions.

KRÜ Blaze are the 2026 VALORANT Game Changers Championship winners. They edged Gentle Mates GC 3-2 at the Riot Games Arena in São Paulo on 1 November. No Latin American team had lifted the title before. No team had ever won it from the lower bracket either.

The event ran from 22 October, with 10 teams competing. Gentle Mates earned US$100,000 as runners-up. Shopify Rebellion Gold took US$70,000 for third place and MIBR GC US$50,000 for fourth.

KRÜ took the long route. They beat Gen.G GC 2-1 in the upper-bracket quarter-finals on 23 October. A 2-0 loss to Shopify Rebellion Gold on 27 October then dropped them into the lower bracket. They answered with clean sweeps of Team Liquid Brazil and MIBR GC. On 31 October they beat Shopify Rebellion Gold 3-1 in the best-of-five lower-bracket final.

The grand final swung back and forth. Gentle Mates took Haven 13-5 before KRÜ levelled on Abyss by the same score. KRÜ led the third map 10-2 at half-time. Gentle Mates fought back, but KRÜ closed it out 14-12 in overtime. Gentle Mates then won Split 13-8 to force a decider. KRÜ led 11-5 on Ascent and won it by the same margin as Split.

Liquipedia named KRÜ’s Argentine player tok1o as the event’s MVP. Brazilian teammates antG and none became the first Brazilians to win an international tournament held in São Paulo.

The result breaks a pattern. Before 2026 the title went to G2 Gozen for Europe in 2022, Shopify Rebellion for North America in 2023 and 2024, and Team Liquid Brazil in 2025. KRÜ’s own record at the event had improved steadily. They finished 7th–8th in 2022 and 5th–6th in each of the next two years. Last year they came fourth.

For European fans, it was a painful near miss. Gentle Mates GC arrived as EMEA’s top seed on circuit points. The team had not lost a series in São Paulo before the final, according to Esports News UK.

It capped a strong debut season in the circuit. Gentle Mates won EMEA Stage 1 by sweeping G2 Gozen 3-0 on 22 February. They lost the Stage 2 final to SK Nebula on 24 May without winning a map. On 30 August they lost the Stage 3 final to G2 Gozen in a fifth map. Silver in São Paulo leaves them with one title from four finals this year.

After a lower bracket run in São Paulo, the LATAM squad claimed the #VCTGameChangers Championship trophy! pic.twitter.com/YeSeb10TZc

— VCT Pacific (@vctpacific) November 1, 2026

The São Paulo final also closes a format. KRÜ are the last team to lift the trophy at a separate event of its own. For the first time, the Game Changers Championship will finish at Champions. Under Riot’s 2027 plan, non-partner teams that qualify for the Game Changers Championship will receive an extra US0,000 incentive. VALORANT Champions 2027 is scheduled for 16 September to 10 October in Austin.

#4288. The Duskbloods Delayed To 2027 So FromSoftware Can Adjust 'Game Rules And Balancing'

While the 2025 reveal of the Switch 2 came with many surprises, none were as unexpected as The Duskbloods. It's a Switch 2 exclusive, multiplayer-only title from FromSoftware, the developer behind games like Dark Souls and Elden Ring; in other words, not your typical Nintendo game. While The Duskbloods was originally scheduled to launch sometime this year, today the developer announced it's pushing the game's launch to 2027.

According to a post on The Duskbloods' X account, the main reason for the delay was balance-related. Here's the full statement:

While development of "The Duskbloods" is at the final adjustment stage, we have made the decision to move the launch window to 2027. We apologize to players who have been kindly awaiting the release of this title and thank you for your patience and support. During the network test, we saw active interest in the core concepts of the game, including combat, strategic depth, and player expression. To further enhance these aspects, we have decided to move the launch, allowing time for final adjustments to game rules and balancing.

We attended a hands-on preview session earlier this year and came away very positive, and sentiment was similar following the game's closed network test (that is, when the servers were working properly). It's not surprising that the devs have changes in mind following so much public feedback, though it is a little surprising that it will take until sometime next year for those adjustments to be complete.

To tide you over until the game's launch, check out our in-depth preview impressions or watch the video above to hear our live commentary over gameplay footage. You can also hear us discuss the game on our podcast, The Game Informer Show.

#4287. Invictus Gaming beat Top Esports 3-1 to reach first Worlds semi-final since 2019

Invictus Gaming knocked out fellow LPL side Top Esports in the opening quarter-final of Worlds 2026 in Allen, Texas. The result guarantees China a semi-final place after the LPL's 0-4 start in the Swiss Stage.

Invictus Gaming are through to the last four of Worlds 2026. They beat fellow LPL side Top Esports in the opening match of the Knockout Stage. The series was played at the Credit Union of Texas Event Center in Allen, Texas, on 3 November (US time).

The win guarantees China a semi-final place. That matters after the LPL’s 0-4 start in the Swiss Stage. IG now meet either Gen.G or LYON. Gen.G beat IG 1-0 in the Swiss Stage and finished it with a perfect 3-0 record.

TES played the event without ZUIAN. On 6 October the club announced that Bai ‘369’ Jia-Hao would move into the starting line-up because of visa problems affecting ZUIAN.

The stand-in still made his mark. IG won Game 1 after building a gold lead of more than 10,000. TES levelled in Game 2 when 369, on Renekton, killed JiaQi and TheShy on his own late in the game. IG then took the next two games to close out the series.

Every Knockout Stage match is a single-elimination best-of-five played with Fearless Draft. The two sides knew each other well. They met twice in best-of-five series in September. IG won 3-2 in the LPL Split 3 playoffs on 5 September. TES won 3-1 in the LPL Regional Finals on 17 September.

The prize money gap is now fixed. Worlds 2026 has a total prize pool of US$5,000,000, with US$1,000,000 for the winner. Each losing semi-finalist receives US$400,000, so IG are guaranteed at least that sum.

IG’s run began with a mid-season rescue. The team started LPL Split 3 in the Nirvana Group. The club then asked TheShy and Rookie, who were both on a break, to come back. The pair helped the side qualify for Worlds. Both won the 2018 world title with IG.

TheShy said he had promised IG’s CEO he would help if asked. “I came back to keep my word,” he said after the series.

#4286. Killing Floor 3 Studio Announces Layoffs After Publishing Hire Spree

Lauren has experience in the gaming and esports space, writing news, guides, features, reviews, lists, conducting interviews, and more. Before joining the team at DualShockers, Lauren was a Features Writer at Adventure Gamers, a Guides Writer at Gameranx, as well as contributing as a News Writer at PCInvasion and Daily

Layoffs are always devastating for the video game industry and the people affected. Unfortunately, they have become all too common, and whether it’s a small studio or a large household name, it seems nobody is safe in today’s climate.

Tripwire Interactive, best known for the Killing Floor series, is the latest studio to be hit by layoffs. The studio was founded back in 2005, and Embracer Group acquired Tripwire Interactive through its former subsidiary, Saber Interactive, in 2022.

In our Killing Floor 3 Review, we go over what could have worked and what didn't in the end for Tripwire's latest game.

In a statement published on the official Tripwire Interactive X account, the studio says it “has undergone a workforce reduction, affecting 36 talented people across our studio. This was certainly not an easy decision, but unfortunately, a necessary one for the organization.”

Tripwire Interactive describes the impacted employees as “truly great people who are exceptional at their roles,” and vows to “help and support these individuals with compassion and dignity during transition.”

The team will continue to focus on Maneater 2, which was officially announced as part of Sony’s September State of Play. It’s expected to launch sometime in 2027.

As the name suggests, Maneater 2 is the sequel to 2021’s Maneater, an action-packed RPG where you are the biggest threat in the open-world oceans that you’ll traverse. There are new evolutions, discoveries to be made, and a whole lot of opportunities to become the villain.

It has also been confirmed that work will continue on Killing Floor 3, as the developers try to salvage the rocky start the game had when it was released back in July 2025. Killing Floor 3 reviews remain mixed among critics and players, and updates are still rolling out, containing new content and fixes.

This isn’t the first time this year that Tripwire Interactive has held layoffs. On March 4, the studio cut its workforce by 23 people, meaning this new round of layoffs brings Tripwire Interactive’s total this year to 59. Only time will tell if any of Tripwire Interactive’s projects will suffer from delays as a result of these layoffs.

Similar to this instance, a real reason wasn’t provided for the March 4 layoffs, instead citing: “As the gaming industry continues to evolve, so do the needs of our studios, which means understanding our long-term strategy and aligning with business realities where needed in order to stay focused on our key creative goals.”

Tripwire Interactive describes the impacted employees as “truly great people who are exceptional at their roles,” and vows to “help and support these individuals with compassion and dignity during transition.”

On November 4, 2026, Tripwire Presents, the publishing sector of Tripwire Interactive, announced that it would be expanding its business to include scaled publishing support for indie developers to help put the spotlight on indie titles from across a variety of genres. The purpose of the initiative is to provide greater visibility for self-published indie games that Tripwire believes fans will enjoy.

It has been confirmed that Tripwire Presents will continue to go ahead with their plans, and the games that have already been chosen are The Boss Gangster: Criminal Empire, Starforged Legacy, Mars Attracts, One-Eyed Likho, and Eslabong.

This round of redundancies adds another to the tally of alarmingly large video game industry layoffs just this year alone. Other examples include Sucker Punch making staff cuts shortly after the launch of the Complete Edition of Ghost of Yōtei, and, of course, the mass layoffs conducted by XBOX.

Another three rounds of XBOX layoffs are slated to begin this month and last into the new year.

#4285. Kettle Street sends you searching for a missing cat in its new Missing Abra event

Where’s Wally (Waldo, if you grew up in the US) only works because everyone’s staring at the same page, so someone can point and the rest of you can pretend you’d nearly got there. Kettle Street, the cosy British life sim, is taking a page out of that book for their latest event, Missing Abra. Claire’s calico cat has gone missing somewhere in town, and you need to help find it.

You find her by wandering Kettleby, and once you spot her, you take a photo with a new camera. She hides somewhere different in each person’s town, though. A mate who found her yesterday can’t tell you where yours is, and neither can we. No guides will help with this one.

I think that makes it more fun. Hunts with fixed answers last about as long as it takes someone to post the answer online. Then, you’re just following directions. Moving Abra around makes the search distinctive. She’s also patchy and not stripy - keep an eye out.

Kettle Street launched on Android in October and reached iOS a week or so later. AssurePath Games, the tiny Manchester studio behind it, has been adding something to town most weeks since.

The next big addition is The Business Expansion, still in development, which now has a first-look trailer. You rent a market stall through the letting agent, work your way up to a shop on the High Street, and do the work behind the counter yourself.

Missing Abra begins on November 12th. Kettle Street is free for your first week in town, then a one-off £4.99 in the UK, with no ads or subscriptions. And for the record, stripes would’ve helped, Abra.

#4284. After 15 years, The Sims' best spin-off finally gets its due follow-up in The Sims 4: Royalty & Legacy

The Sims Medieval had a short but powerful run back in 2011, and now many of its best features are finally coming to the main franchise.

The Sims 4 developers recently promised an exciting year for the game, and the franchise as a whole, and we just got an early look at one of those first events. After some light teasing, the developer unveiled Royalty & Legacy, the game’s next expansion.

Royalty & Legacy’s first trailer debuted on Thursday, revealing a February 12 release date, and showing off the expansion for the first time.

There’s a lot going on in Royalty & Legacy, which is priced $40. For one, it introduces a new world, Ondarion, which is going to be the setting for your kingdom, as you join a race for the throne. The expansion introduces Dynasty and Nobility - two new systems you can use to create your own world of royal shenanigans.

Ondarion is made up of three neighborhoods (regions). Each region has a unique theme and culture, and they’re each ruled by a Dynasty. Dambele is a place that prioritises art and community. Verdemar is a chaotic world of outlaws and nobles. Finally, Bellacorde is an extravagant region known for opulence and romance.

Speaking of building places, Royalty & Legacy also adds a new Lot type, The Backroom Lot. It serves two functions that change with the time of day. For instance, it can be a library or gym in the morning, and shift into a night club at night. Dambele has its own library-turned-rave, for instance.

At the heart of Ondarion are all the possible fantasy lives and stories you can live. The Sims calls them Powershifts, and they include some well-known Arthurian fantasies and other, more silly ones.

Swordsmanship is the new 10-level skill arriving with the expansion, which further plays into those fantasies by letting your Sims duel. There are even Swordsmanship Tournaments you can watch take place across every neighborhood in Ondarion.

Then there are Secret Passageways, which let you speed up moving across the new regions. They essentially let your Sims teleport between designated passageways, either on their own lots, or other lots in the world. Some of these are hidden for you to find, while others you can create.

In terms of new careers, there’s the Noble Career, where your Sim can rise through several Noble Rankings by doing basically what nobles had to do in the middle ages to earn favour.

The aforementioned Dynasty System is how you can join any of Ondarion’s existing families, or start your own. You actually have a lot of say in what goes on, including the usual business of appointing heirs.

Of course, no royal roleplay would be complete without scandals, which is where the Scandals System comes in. Through it, you can create stories to discredit others, or even topple an entire dynasty.

In November, you may recall The Sims 4 introducing new free items inspired by West African culture. In creating that content, EA worked with a group of Simmers who have direct ties to West African countries.

The group’s guidance was once again utilised to build the Dambele neighborhood in this expansion, and some of the lots around the world of Ondarion were even created by members of the group.

While you wait for Royalty & Legacy to actually arrive, there’s more in The Sims 4 you can jump in right now. The game recently kicked off a collaboration with fashion brand Coach that brought several free items to Create a Sim, and Build Buy. That arrived alongside a free update, which already makes for a busy start of the year for The Sims 4.

#4283. Assassin’s Creed Franchise Update Reveals Codename Hexe News Coming Next Year, New Game Plus for Valhalla, And Confirms No New Remakes

Ubisoft has released a fall update on the Assassin’s Creed franchise, providing news big and small on its flagship series. The news includes updates for existing games and smaller but significant insights on the various upcoming Assassin’s Creed games previously announced.

In terms of current games, Assassin’s Creed Valhalla is getting a long-requested New Game Plus thanks to a new update coming on November 5. This means you can start a fresh game while bringing over your progression items/level from your previous playthrough. This update will also introduce the following features:

This news comes a few days after New Game Plus arrived in Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced.

Codname Invictis, a PvP multiplayer game, remains in development as Ubisoft shares it has incorporated feedback from players who, according to Ubisoft, “saw great potential in the foundations but wanted more of the pillars that define Assassin's Creed.” To this end, Ubisoft has spent months reworking Invictis to reflect this vague feedback and say the game is “now evolving in an exciting direction that better reflects those pillars while staying true to its multiplayer ambitions.”

As for the next single-player Assassin’s Creed, Codename Hexe, Ubisoft says it will share the next major update on this game in 2027. First announced in 2022, Codename Hexe is set during the 17th-century reign of the Holy Roman Empire, and the era's witch hunts will play a significant role.

With the release of Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced earlier this year, Ubisoft has given fans what they'll likely see as a disappointing update on potential future remakes: “One thing we want to be transparent about today is that we currently have no other Assassin's Creed remake actively in development. Our teams are already focused on the next chapter of Assassin's Creed titles, including projects you haven't heard about yet, featuring new settings and stories.”

However, Ubisoft adds that this door isn’t closed for good. “Like many of you, we love the idea of revisiting our classic titles, and we'll keep exploring opportunities to bring older titles back,” says Ubisoft.

Ubisoft’s next update concerns the live-action Assassin's Creed series in production for Netflix. They say the show is “nearing completion” in Rome and that award-winning composer Hannah Peel (Insomnia, Rogue Agent, Game of Thrones: The Last Watch) is composing the score.

Lastly, Ubisoft teases big celebrations are planned for 2027, which marks the 20th anniversary of the Assassin's Creed franchise. It's keeping details to itself for now, but states it's "preparing a year of reveals, updates, rewards, and community moments. "

For more on Assassin's Creed, check out our review of Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced.

#4282. Forgotten Memories: Definitive Edition is now free forever on iOS and Android

Free forever is a big promise, but Psychose Interactive has a fairly good reason for making it. Forgotten Memories: Definitive Edition, the studio’s survival horror from 2015, is now free on iOS and Android. No, this isn’t a weekend giveaway or one of Epic Games' weekly freebies. It’s staying that way.

You play as Rose Hawkins, who wakes up in an abandoned asylum while searching for a missing girl called Eden. It’s slow, third-person 90s-style horror, with puzzles, a torch and never quite enough ammo.

The asylum is split into different wings, and most of your time will be spent figuring out which locked door to open next. Our original review compared it closer to a point-and-click adventure, and with that many keys and locked doors, it’s probably true. The scares tend to land on the way back, once you’ve got what you came for and have to walk past the mannequins again.

It’s properly old-fashioned about the rest. You fight with a lead pipe and a bit of timing, and the torch battery runs down. Saving originally meant finding a computer and spending one of a limited stock of floppy disks, in the style of early Resident Evil, so dying could cost you half an hour.

Forgotten Memories: Remastered smooths some of the bugs out. It’s the rebuilt version that launched on mobile two years ago, with new lighting and checkpoint saves.

#4278. Tomorrow's Battlefield 6 patch somehow makes jets more useless, improves armor bar visibility in Redsec

The first Battlefield 6 patch of the year is almost here, bringing a smattering of changes, including one that doesn't quite make sense.

Battlefield 6’s promised, season-extending update has been officially detailed. The patch, version 1.1.3.5, arrives tomorrow, January 20 right when Season 1 was supposed to end. Part of the update’s goal is to extend the current season, until Season 2 kicks off in the middle of February.

Update 1.1.3.5 does, of course, have a change log of its own that goes beyond just the season’s extension, but the changes fall somewhere between not very exciting, and a bit puzzling.

Patch 1.1.3.5 is, for all intents and purposes, a smaller update. When Battlefield Studios announced it earlier last week, the developer didn’t promise any major changes or fixes, so expectations never got out of hand.

The patch is mainly made up of bug fixes, but it does have three key areas of improvements to gameplay. There’s a big focus on melee combat, how responsive/unresponsive it is with the various melee tools, and how melee behaviour interacts with sprinting and other animations.

The end result should be faster attack speeds for the knife, and clearer wind-up animations for both the knife and the sledgehammer. The timing dictating when melee damage gets credited has also been made more consistent in different environments.

Interestingly, sprint is now only interrupted when the melee attack reaches its target. As it stands, sprinting is only interrupted after the full duration of the animation has been completed, which adds to the that perceived feeling of sluggishness.

The other major, and arguably most confusing is the nerf to jet cannons. The patch is going to make jets far less stronger against other air vehicles, requiring 40% more hits to destroy a target. This is puzzling because jets - and air vehicles in general - are already the least survivable in Battlefield 6.

And, considering how the rest of a jet's arsenal is either situational or nearly ineffective, the cannons were really the one guaranteed way of downing other air vehicles, so long as you manage to land your shots consistently. While the change is wellmeaning, the percentage will likely be reduced in future patches.

Finally, the update makes a few refinements to UI across the game, though mainly aimed at Redsec and modes where players wear armor. Armor bar visibility has been improved, and there’s a fix for the annoying bug that sometimes caused the armor bar to disappear every few seconds.

Gen.G beat LYON 3-0 in Allen, Texas, removing North America's last team from Worlds 2026. The LCK top seed are now one series from a first Worlds final, with a revived Invictus Gaming in the way.

Gen.G swept LYON in the second Worlds 2026 quarter-final in Allen, Texas. The defeat removes North America’s last team from the tournament. The LCK top seed now face Invictus Gaming in a best-of-five semi-final on Saturday, starting at 16:00 Central Time.

Reaching the last four secures Gen.G at least third or fourth place. That is a familiar stopping point for the organisation. It has finished third or fourth at four of its last five Worlds and has never played in a Worlds final, GosuGamers reported.

The stakes go beyond one team. Gen.G entered the tournament as the LCK’s top seed. Korean sides are chasing a fifth Summoner’s Cup in a row.

Their opponents bring their own history. Invictus Gaming beat Top Esports 3-1 in the opening quarter-final. That put iG into their first Worlds semi-final since 2019. TheShy and Rookie, who won Worlds with iG in 2018, are back in the last four.

The money rises sharply from here. Worlds 2026 carries a US$5,000,000 prize pool. The champion takes US$1,000,000 (20%), and the runner-up receives US$800,000.

For LYON, the exit still marks clear progress. They go out in joint fifth to eighth place and collect a share of the prize money. GosuGamers called it easily the organisation’s best Worlds finish. In four earlier appearances, LYON never placed higher than 17th.

Their elimination also changes the shape of the event. North America will have no representative in the semi-finals or the Grand Final. The remaining matches in Allen will be contested without a team from the region.

The arena covers 15,000 sq ft. It has a 17-metre-wide LED screen, a 200-seat viewing area and a bar. Students can get discounted tickets.

Whether Gen.G or iG make it to that final will be settled in Allen on Saturday. The Sunderland watch party runs from 5:30pm on the day of the final until 1:00am on 15 November.

As promised, Battlefield Labs is coming back to bring us a preview of some of Battlefield 6’s upcoming Season 2 content.

Battlefield 6’s Season 2 was recently pushed back by a month to give Battlefield Studios time to polish up its content. Now, the developer has revealed how it plans to use some of that time, and the first port of call is Battlefield Labs.

As discussed in the initial delay message, BF Studios wants the community’s involvement earlier and more consistently in the development of future content. This includes Season 2, of course, and a big component of what it’s bringing to the game is headed to Labs.

The first Battlefield Labs session kicking off soon will focus on Contaminated, one of the new maps coming to Battlefield 6 with Season 2. BF Studios says the map falls between Eastwood and Mirak Valley, in terms of size.

The blog post even likened it to Battlefield 1’s St. Quentin Scar, and Battlefield 5’s Arras. Although we’ve yet to actually play it, the size and description do sound really well, especially in a game as starved of big maps as Battlefield 6 currently is.

Another thing BF Studios wants to test is the way ground vehicle gameplay and aerial presence interact with infantry combat, which is pretty standard for most Battlefield maps. Interestingly, there appears to be some sort of mechanic unique to Contaminated that the developer also wants to evaluate.

More Labs sessions are planned, including one that will show off new gameplay tools and vehicles. The AH-6 Little Bird helicopter was specifically namedropped, which makes sense given that it’s going to be part of Season 2’s content.

Battlefield Labs sessions will also extend beyond the biggest-ticket items of maps and vehicles. BF Studios said we should expect tests of upcoming features, like the Aircraft Radar, as part of a list of other air combat updates.

Ground vehicles, and they way the various rockets interact with them, will also be evaluated in a different session, with specific adjustments planned for RPGs and TOWs. And, of course, the work to improve and perfect hit reg remains ongoing, and future tweaks will go through Labs first.

There’s even more exciting news for fans of big maps, as the blog post also confirmed that Battlefield 4’s Golmud Railway is currently in the works, planned to go live in a future season. Golmud Railway will show up early in Labs, and you can expect it to evolve over multiple sessions.

For context, when it does arrive in Battlefield 6, Golmud Railway will be the largest map in the game, which is saying something. Though the map is beloved by vehicle players, it has its issues elsewhere, and BF Studios says it will be looking at all that when it creates the BF6, emphasising that it won’t be a simple port of the BF4 original.

Finally, the post throws a bone to Redsec battle royale players still waiting for a Solo mode. BF Studios continues to test the idea internally, but it’s taking a while. Needless to say, there are so many aspects that need to be considered. Game pace, balance, player survivability, match flow just to name a few.

Redsec BR was built with squads in mind, so that task is extra challenging. Though the developer didn’t say when we can expect Solos to arrive in Labs, players will get a chance to experience it before it enters the live game.
