#4221. You're not crazy, trying to heal in Nioh 3 sometimes doesn't work - and Team Ninja is fixing it

One of the more insidiously aggravating bugs in Nioh 3 makes it so the game ignores you when you try to use elixirs, but hopefully not for long.

Nioh 3 has received a hot new update that brings plenty of bug fixes to very specific issues, but it also implements fixes for a few of the most common - and incredibly annoying - bugs. Patch 1.03.01 arrived earlier on all platforms, and it comes with a chunky set of notes.

This latest update, predictably, doesn’t add any gameplay features, but some of the included fixes will absolutely delight - or vindicate - so many of the game’s millions of players.

There’s plenty to go through in the patch notes published today for update 1.03.01, but the most impactful is a fix for an issue that “sometimes made it impossible to use elixirs during battle.” This is only a partial fix, but if you ran into the problem of smashing that shortcut button and not seeing your character play the healing animation, you’ll be glad to see it.

This is a problem myself and others have faced, especially in boss fights. You can even see the shortcut register your button press and proceed to ignore you. Another partial fix has been made to an issue that caused the game to crash. Team Ninja didn’t share specifics on that, and though Nioh 3 has been fairly stable for me in 70+ hours, it has definitely crashed a few times.

If you’ve been playing since launch, you likely have - or know someone who has - run into issues with save file corruption and other weird bugs around certain trackable items within save files.

Team Ninja already rolled out a couple of fixes there, and this latest one specifically targets losing valuables during Myths. If your save file has been affected, the game will now check and recover what was lost. Even more interesting is that the game will now automatically create a backup copy of your save data any time you load a save.

If you’ve made it into the Eternal Rift, you’ll be happy to know that today’s update takes care of a few progression blockers, and fixes an issue that allowed some players to obtain certain items before they were supposed to, locking themselves out.

One of the more amusing fixes concerns Mujina, who had a tendency to respawn if you prayed at a Shrine after opening a chest it was hiding in, which made it appear far more often than a mimic should.

Finally, there’s a set of fixes that address bugs (and exploits) when using specific Martial Art with certain weapons. There are a few fixes to AI, Myths, and one problem with the Minamoto no Yoritomo boss fight that made it impossible to interrupt him, even after he runs out of Ki.

Hit the link at the top for the full change log, and check out our Nioh 3 gameplay tips if you haven’t already. You should also change these settings ASAP, as they’re going to make your life much easier and save you a lot of time.

#4220. Everything In The GTA 6 Selfridges Collection Is Available Online

You have almost certainly seen the stunning new GTA 6 display in London’s Selfridges, filled with new merch, some of which can’t be found anywhere else. There is good news for those of you who won’t be popping to the UK anytime soon, though - everything in the new collection is available to buy online.

There are 62 items in the GTA 6 x Selfridges collection, some of which are also available through the Rockstar website, others that aren’t - and may never be - available elsewhere. The GTA 6 varsity jacket, the most expensive item in the collection, falls into that latter category.

Priced at $3,025, the jacket is black and white with some rather colorful Vice City-themed embroidery on its back and up and down its sleeves. The good news and bad news for those of you tempted by it is that the jacket appears to have already sold out. Bad news because you can’t have one, good because you just saved yourself $3,000.

T-shirts, hats, bags, and more have been added to what is now a far more full GTA 6 merch store.

There is a second, all-black, considerably cheaper varsity jacket with Vice City across the chest. That one costs a measly $2,115. For those of you not interested in spending multiple current-gen consoles worth of money on a single piece of GTA 6 merch, most of the other items available won’t require you to not pay your mortgage for a couple of months.

A lot of those cheaper items are the same ones you can buy through Rockstar. T-shirts and caps with Rockstar and GTA 6 logos, for the most part, and I would advise buying them through Rockstar if you can. The T-shirts, for example, are $35 when bought directly from Rockstar, but $67 at Selfridges for what I’m almost certain are the same items.

You might catch out some casuals in-store with those inflated prices, but you won’t be catching us, or most others shopping for GTA 6 merch online.

There is a lot of cool stuff at Selfridges that you can’t find anywhere else, for any price. A GTA 6 basketball, a dartboard, and some beach towels sporting the VI from the GTA 6 logo. There’s even merch themed after some of the game’s fictional sports teams and brands, which might be the best of this collection.

There’s a ton of merch dedicated to the Vice City Manatees, including a football and a plush of the team’s manatee mascot. The Vice City Narcos, GTA 6’s basketball team, also has lots of merch available. Plus lots of items that have been designed to look like you bought them from Burger Shot, a chain of fast food restaurants you’ll be able to visit in GTA 6.

That includes a $115 pair of slacks that are part of the Burger Shot uniform.

The collection also includes a selection of “I Love VC” items that are designed to look like the I Love NYC stuff you can buy on every street corner in New York City. You can also pick up clothes adorned with GTA postcards, enamel pins, magnets, silk scarves, keychains, the first ashtray I’ve seen on sale for about 20 years, a members-only jacket, a luggage tag, and a money clip.

You know what, I lied. There aren’t 62 items in the Selfridges GTA 6 collection; there are 63. The $3,025 jacket isn’t the most expensive thing on sale either. No, it’s actually the Vice City Grotti Cheetah in the store window. That’ll cost you a cool £1 million, or roughly $1.34 million. I'm assuming there's just one of those, but at the time of typing this, it is still available.

Just like Red Dead Redemption 2, GTA 6 is getting a collector's bundle instead of an edition featuring the game.

#4219. Void/Breaker Review – Chaos Is The Point

Many games tout impressive destruction systems under the hood, but few implement it as well as Void/Breaker. The ruin is visually spectacular, sure – who doesn’t love to watch buildings crumble because of your grenade or gravity-thrown explosives? But importantly, it’s a critical aspect of Void/Breaker’s roguelite design. Enemies caught beneath falling rubble become instantly staggered, and that’s your moment to kill. Grenades do this too, as do most items you throw at the hostile AI machinery trying to end your run, creating a vortex of shifting priorities as you dash, jump, and shoot at sequential staggered enemies in your sightlines. Countless weapon mods and permutations make fewer than a dozen weapons feel like hundreds in your arsenal, adding even more blissful chaos to the mix. Though it can be difficult at times, if you can see through the literal remains of your destruction, one of the year’s most engaging shooters awaits.

Void/Breaker wastes no time getting a gun in your hand. An AI voice in your head wants your help escaping a simulation where thousands of runners attempt to reach the end of multi-arena stages to defeat a boss. He asks that you simply follow the simulation’s commands; meanwhile, he uses the data you collect along the way to find new exits for you and him. The storytelling style is very reminiscent of Valve’s Portal. Something much larger is at play here, but it’s worth discovering for yourself.

This narrative framework supports the game’s roguelite structure. Mechanically, however, you enter various themed digital stages, from liminal spaces to beaches to snow-capped cliffs and more, and attempt to survive. Most arenas consist of a couple of starkly white structures that your grenades and thrown explosives can topple (ideally onto waves of enemies below). Learning the language of Void/Breaker means constantly scanning your field of view for explosives and structures practically begging to come down, and then eyeing neon-green bars above enemies that tell you they’re staggered and ready for a quick kill. Developer Stubby Games throws plenty of wrenches into this formula, like armored foes and electrostatic enemies you must melee first, and elite bots that will have you on the back foot, but for the most part, Void/Breaker’s formula is “Break stuff, then kill.”

The game emphasizes explosives and bringing buildings down, but your guns do most of the killing; you can only select one weapon per run. You choose from a pistol, shotgun, machine gun, sniper, and more, and each has its perks (though once I unlocked the SMG, I rarely picked anything else). There’s no sense overthinking your weapon, though, because the dozens of mods you pick up each run determine its effectiveness. As you pick up more schematics, the pool of mods you find in chests or drop from enemies expands, and soon your gun fires corrosive acid, electricity, fire, projectile missiles, and more. Not to mention, mods change how the gun fires, how much damage certain bullets do, recoil, accuracy, and just about any other stat you associate with firing a video game gun. Wild combinations are easy to create, and a unique mod-stacking mechanic that can double or triple effectiveness adds a light touch of puzzle design to this otherwise straight shooter.

Stubby Games smartly emphasizes player expression, never getting in the way of the zanier combinations available to players. The SMG I used to beat the final boss featured mods that made each bullet electric, shot missiles with each shot, covered each bullet in a destructive orb, and featured a ricochet perk that made each bullet bounce off walls and split into even more bullets. I’m thankful for mid-run saves because this SMG permutation, paired with an ability mod that let me throw infinite grenades for a limited time, filled my screen with so much destruction that the entire game crashed. I’d usually bemoan such a thing, but I couldn’t help but laugh. I pushed my PC to its limit with my on-screen chaos.

Boss fights leave a little to be desired – I rarely died because of their simple bullet-hell arenas. Instead, most runs ended because, after bringing down every structure around me, I’d get so lost in the chaos that I wouldn't realize I was stuck in debris while enemies swarmed my location. As stunning as it is to see so much happening on screen, it can be hard to understand what is going on during the most chaotic moments.

Between enemy-filled arenas en route to a stage’s end boss, you might find a shop to buy more mods, ominous obelisks with risk-reward propositions (gain a lot of health or lose half your health, for example), optional trials, and strange phenomena that transport you to different locations. These moments are quick breaks in between bouts of adrenaline-fueled shooter action that I always welcomed – enemies can be relentless, especially as new types are introduced in each stage.

The rest of the Void/Breaker package offers few genre surprises. You can upgrade various traits between runs, research new mod schematics to add to the random pool, purchase new weapons, and discover fun secrets. You can unlock shortcuts, glean in-world information from computer terminals, and hear intriguing dialogue barks from the AI partner who needs your help. It’s all standard stuff for the rogue genre, but if anything, its simplicity pushes you back to the meat and potatoes of this shooter.

Void/Breaker’s shorter runtime – I rolled credits at 12 hours – ensures nothing gets too repetitive in its roguelite structure, but an expansive endgame promises even more to engage with, like different run modifications you can enable to make an already chaotic shooter even more anarchic. I’ll certainly be running it back (again and again) to see what other disruptions I can bring to this AI-simulated adventure. It’s hard not to when destruction feels this good.

#4218. Genshin Impact Luna 5 takes the squad back to Mondstadt, finally makes Varka playable

Genshin Impact's next update will have you reminiscing about the good ol' days of... 2020.

The latest big content update has been revealed for HoYoverse's breakout game, Genshin Impact. Version Luna 5, which has the unusually long and needlessly layered title — Song of the Welkin Moon: Variation - Homeward, He Who Caught the Wind — is set to arrive February 25.

This one is a bit of a nostalgia play, taking everyone back to Mondstadt, the place where you may remember taking your first steps. And, as with any good return to the ol’ hunting grounds, come familiar characters, too.

The big new arrival is Varka, who joins as a playable character for the first time. Varka, Grand Master of the Knights of Favonius, is a character whose debut has been long-awaited. He is a 5-Star Anemo Claymore wielder with a dual-wield combat style, capable of dealing two different types of Elemental damage. His addition means that there's now finally a burly 5-Star male character of each elemental type... do with that information what you will.

Varka's dual-wielding combat style allows him to deal two different types of Elemental damage at the same time. The way it works is that his Elemental Skill boosts the damage of his regular attacks, but it also converts the damage type of his right-hand claymore to match his teammates’ elements (Pyro, Hydro, Electro, or Cryo). The left-hand claymore always deals Anemo damage.

The more normal attacks you use, the more frequently he can activate a special Elemental Skill, or trigger a Charged Attack that doesn’t consume stamina. He can also rely on the Hexerei effect to trigger more instances of Elemental Skill, as well as Charged Attacks, making him a monster damage-dealer.

Varka, of course, has been a staple member of the cast, featuring in both the original story in a small cameo, as well as taking a bigger role in the recent Nod-Krai chapters. With the return to Mondstadt, his playable debut makes sense. His Story Quest will shed light on his encounter with the Wild Hunt, and the Great Wolf King of the North

The reruns for this version are going to be Flins — who will be available in the first phase of Event Wishes — as well as Skirk and Escoffier in the second phase. You can also look forward to the return of the Chronicled Wish with Mondstadt characters.

Staying on the theme of reminiscence, the big event in Luna 5 is centered around revisiting memories from the beginning of your time with Genshin Impact, and reuniting with old friends. In Echoes of Memory, you’ll witness familiar scenes that have been changed slightly, and you’ll need to use the Spotter Kamera to detect and record those differences.

The Knights of Favonius are hosting several other activities for everyone to take part in, including an event that lets you catch up with old friends over drinks which you make for them.

Outside of events, there’s a new set of Gliding and Combat Challenges. And, of course, there are new minigames that you can relax with. The Kamera is being utilised yet again, and this time you can use to capture sights from your time in spots across Natlan, Fontaine, and Sumeru. There’s also… a horde mode of a sort, where you fend off waves of enemies.

#4217. Nioh 3 is, unsurprisingly, the fastest-selling game in the series with over a million units sold

Nioh 3 has taken the Nioh franchise to new heights, delivering its biggest-ever launch.

Even before the game came out, it was pretty easy to guess that Nioh 3 would be a hit. From the word of mouth leading up to launch, to the well-received free demo, there was little chance the action RPG wasn’t going to be a major deal.

Today, publisher Koei Tecmo has announced that the game has officially passed over one million copies sold worldwide across PC, and PlayStation 5. This makes it the fastest in the Nioh franchise to reach this milestone.

As a result of this fantastic launch, Nioh 3 has now pushed overall Nioh franchise sales to be over 10 million, which includes the original Nioh as well as Nioh 2. Today’s news comes just two weeks after the game arrived on PC, and PS5.

On Steam, where it’s available on PC, it shot up the Steam charts, and immediately broke the series’ previous best peak concurrent player count record. From there, the numbers kept growing, leading up to a stellar weekend where it peaked at 88,045 concurrent players on Steam, double that of its launch day.

This now stands as the largest for any Nioh game on Steam, and though we don’t have insight into how well it’s doing on PS5 specifically, it still shows that the Nioh series continues to grow.

Nioh 3 builds on everything the two prior games established, and pushes the series into the semi-open-world realm, with several larger maps that each cover a period of time in Japan’s history. In our Nioh 3 review we called it “Team Ninja’s most accomplished action game, and the series’ most accessible.”

#4216. Digimon Alysion Passes 200,000 Registrations With New Rewards Revealed

Digimon isn't a new TCG, but a brand-new mobile version of the game, Digimon Alysion, is coming before the end of 2026, and the pre-registration phase just hit a major milestone.

It's launching in a market stacked with competition, but Digimon has a pretty hardcore fanbase behind it, and this new app will make the game far more accessible to new players who have never played and returning players who haven't engaged with the game for an extended period of time. Fans have been waiting a long time for this game to finally launch, so we expect there is a very good chance that these new milestones will be hit.

Pre-registration for Digimon Alysion started on October 27, 2026, meaning this huge milestone has taken just over a month to achieve, and developer Bandai Namco isn't stopping there. There are rewards laid out to cover up to 400,000 pre-registered users, ranging from in-game tickets to a guaranteed card, Omnimon.

The game is available to pre-register on the App Store and Google Play, and the total number of registrations covers the cumulative figures from both platforms.

Four rewards from previous milestones are locked in and will be delivered to every player who pre-registers when they first open the app. These rewards include more of the same, tickets, and guaranteed cards. There is also a separate reward scheme running that is related to the number of players who have joined the official Discord server. If 10,000 members join the community by November 30, all players who log into the game will receive five BD-03 tickets.

Digimon fans will soon have their own Pokemon TCG Pocket competitor.

It's been confirmed that Digimon Alysion includes plenty of single-player content, including a Story Mode where players earn rewards as they get more familiar with the game. From there, multiplayer modes will make up the majority of the game, ranging from casual to competitive modes.

Early looks at the game show a lot of similarities to Yu-Gi-Oh! Master Duel, at least in the way that content is presented and menu navigation works.

#4215. The Sims 4 developer hasn't forgotten about its quality of life commitment, and is back with an update on what to expect in 2026

Maxis has offered some fresh details on its long-running mission to improve player quality of life in The Sims 4.

As the The Sims 4 continues into its second decade, the volume of new content, major expansions, and long-awaited features has grown in lockstep. Unfortunately, that has also meant that, given how old the game is, a few technical problems remain a nuisance.

The effort required to fix them is what led developer Maxis to make a commitment to improve the game’s technical state, and the developer has now returned to update the community on what to expect in 2026.

The quality of life pledge was made in September last year, through the introduction of a roadmap. Since then, the developer issued one update on its progress. Which brings us to this week’s new blog post, which further builds on everything that’s come before.

In the post, Maxis revealed a few key areas it’s going to be focusing on going forward. Though specific release dates for these changes were not shared, the list of issues should resonate with many players, as it covers many often-discussed topics.

The first stage of the new roadmap covers March through August. Over that period, you can expect Sims' autonomy to improve. This goes for things like how they choose locations for certain actions, they way they interact with certain objects, and even how often they interrupt conversations.

The infant and caregiver relationship is being updated, too, in order to improve autonomy and make sure your little Sims don’t miss out on milestones and interactions. That stage of the roadmap also includes fixes for black photo issues, and other crashes and freezing.

The next period takes place September through December, and it includes more interesting changes. One of the goals with this one is to improve Sims’ dining experience, which covers issues around eating and drinking.

Another important area of focus with this stage is family trees, and relationships between members of the same family. Maxis wants to improve the game’s genealogy systems to make relationship tracking across generations more robust so that your family history isn’t lost.

Depending on how the first stage goes, you might see more issues join the list of what the developer is looking at for the second stage of the roadmap.

The good news is that you won’t have to wait too long for the game’s next patch. Due out in March, this next update will feature around 55 fixes, including for some commonly reported issues.

Until then, you may want to check out The Sims 4’s Lost Legacies Event, which is available now until the middle of March. If you picked up the game’s latest expansion, check if you tried those Royalty & Legacy cheats.

#4214. GTA 6 Will Be Playable on XBOX One, According to Rockstar

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

A big part of what’s making the steadily-encroaching release of Grand Theft Auto 6 interesting in the current gaming climate, besides, y’know, being Grand Theft Auto 6, is that it’s only going to be available on consoles, and specifically XBOX and PlayStation family consoles. PC and Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 are being left out in the cold, at least for the time being, although rumors abound that the PC launch may come sooner than expected in order to beat out AI slop knockoffs.

I don’t claim to know all of the precise reasons for this particular launch strategy, beyond perhaps a pursuit for immediate at-launch optimization for the most readily-available consoles. That said, it would seem that, even if you own a particular console from the previous generation, you may still be able to play the game, albeit in a slightly diminished state.

Rockstar announced on its official news blog today that pre-loading for Grand Theft Auto 6 has officially begun, with the many who pre-ordered the game digitally now able to start downloading, and those who purchased codes-in-boxes able to start redeeming them and do the same. Buried within this announcement was a rather unexpected detail: it’ll be possible to play Grand Theft Auto 6 on the previous generation’s XBOX One console.

GTA 6, Rockstar's upcoming open-world adventure, is taking up 210 GB on PlayStation 5.

Here’s the interesting bit: since XBOX Cloud Gaming is also available on the XBOX One console, that means you can, in fact, play Grand Theft Auto 6 on an XBOX One by streaming it. At least as far as I’ve determined, the XBOX One will be the only previous-gen console that will be able to play this brand-new game, and an exceptionally high-end game at that.

Since XBOX Cloud Gaming is also available on the XBOX One console, that means you can, in fact, play Grand Theft Auto 6 on an XBOX One.

Of course, there are some catches here. First, no matter what XBOX console you’re playing on, any instance of Grand Theft Auto 6 played via Cloud Gaming will use XBOX Series S-tier graphical settings, i.e. not the best possible ones. Additionally, as is always the case with cloud streaming, how good the game looks and runs is largely dependent on the quality of your internet connection, so if you’ve got lousy speeds, this isn’t going to work well for you.

As GTA 6's launch approaches, everyone wants part of the PR pie, including internet ISPs.

On a semi-related note, Rockstar also confirmed that Grand Theft Auto 6 will work with Remote Play on both PlayStation and XBOX consoles, for those who want to stream the game from their console to elsewhere in their home.

I probably don’t need to remind anybody of this, but here it is anyway: Grand Theft Auto 6 is officially launching on Thursday, November 19, with the unlock time being whenever the clock strikes midnight in your particular time zone.

Whether through an installed digital copy or, apparently, on an XBOX One via Cloud Gaming, anyone who is interested in this game will, with certainty, be playing it as soon as it launches. I shudder to think what those poor digital storefronts are going to be going through at midnight on the 19th. Maybe wait until after school or work that day before you try to start playing, at least assuming you’re not one of the metric whoa-ton of people who are projected to be calling in sick that day.

Grand Theft Auto 6 is encroaching upon our reality, and upon its advent, there is a non-zero chance life will never be the same. If you’re not too busy playing the game for an indeterminate blur of time, maybe you can check out Rockstar’s official launch party in Miami the following weekend.

A massive music festival will be held in Miami the weekend following the game's release, with numerous big-name performers to participate.

#4213. Father Arrested For Leaving 6-Year-Old Daughter Sleeping In Line For Pokémon Cards

A 35-year-old South Carolina man has been arrested and accused of leaving his 6-year-old daughter asleep while waiting in line for Pokémon cards.

As reported by The Washington Post (thanks, IGN), John-Michael Dooley was waiting outside a Target store with his daughter in Charleston's West Ashley district, where a crowd had gathered hoping to purchase the newly-released Pokémon set. Officers arrived at the store at 2:30am local time after receiving reports of an unattended child.

Witnesses reported that Dooley gave his daughter a pillow and a blanket sometime after 1:00am before leaving her asleep in the line. After he failed to return within an hour, the concerned witnesses contacted the police.

When the man eventually returned to the store, he was arrested. He later admitted to leaving his daughter unattended so that he could keep his place in line while he had gone home. He was subsequently charged with unlawful conduct toward a child, while his daughter was placed in emergency protective custody. Thankfully, she was unharmed.

Many of us here at NL are parents, and so it enrages us to no end that someone would even consider doing this. We're at least relieved that no harm came to the 6-year-old girl, but it could have been much worse.

#4212. Genshin Impact fans on PS4 only have six weeks to find another platform as support winds down with one final update

Premium in-game purchases have now been disabled on PlayStation 4, as one of Genshin's four original launch platforms prepares to get dropped in early April.

Version Luna 5 of Genshin Impact is now live, but it's a bittersweet occasion for fans of HoYoverse's breakout gacha RPG – at the very least, those who are still playing the game on PlayStation 4, which is presumably true of somebody out there.

HoYoverse announced last year that they intended to wind down support for Genshin Impact on PS4, which – alongside PC, Android, and iOS – was one of the launch platforms for the game back in 2020. And with Version Luna 5, those end days are upon us.

The game has already been delisted on the platform since last September, meaning it was no longer available for download and could only be updated by players who already had it installed. But as of today, paid purchases from the in-game store have been disabled on PS4; and in six weeks' time, on approximately April 8, Version Luna 6 will discontinue access to the PS4 version altogether.

In many ways this is unsurprising – Genshin is already available on both PS5 and Xbox Series to sate fans eager to play on console, and the PS4's hardware is increasingly struggling to keep up with this massive open-world game after more than five years of regular updates have ballooned both its file size and technical requirements.

Aptly enough, Luna 5 takes the main story action back to the nation of Mondstadt, the location where the Traveler (and, by extension, the players) took their first steps into the world of Teyvat back in September 2020. It feels like a symbolic last hurrah for the original console home of the game, as does the inclusion of a Chronicled Wish banner focussing on some of Mondstadt's most iconic (read: too old to be meta by now) 5-Star characters – namely Eula, Mona, Albedo, Klee, Diluc, and Jean.

And as the icing on the Tea Break Pancake, this banner is running alongside the long-anticipated introduction of Varka – the Grand Master of the Knights of Favonius who has been a major character in the game's lore from the very beginning, but who only became playable with today's update.

Looking ahead to that post-Luna 6 future, Genshin Impact will still be available on PS5, as well as Xbox Series consoles, PC, and mobile devices – so hopefully anyone who is still playing primarily on PS4 will find another platform they can continue the adventure on by April.

#4211. 10 PS4 Adventure Games Where You’re Actually the Villain

Eric Warner is a Journalist and Multimedia Producer based in New England with over 7 years of experience producing stories for multiple publications

Of all the PlayStation consoles, the PlayStation 2 is widely considered to be the most successful as it still holds the title of being the best-selling game console of all time, with the Nintendo Switch coming close behind as the second best-selling game console.

While the PS2 would see a wide variety of great video games debut on the platform, I would argue that the PlayStation 4 featured a greater variety of titles that, more often than not, featured an overall superior quality compared to their PS2 predecessors.

In one respect, this can be seen in the increased freedom PS4 games offered players, with several adventure and open-world titles granting them the ability to embody villainous, often chaotic and destructive, roles. Watch out for major spoilers for the following titles, if you haven't played these PS4 games!

Traveller's Tales’ LEGO video games are famous for adapting some of cinema’s most famous series in comical LEGO form, but LEGO DC Super-Villains broke that mold by featuring a mostly original story loosely inspired by DC Comics’ Forever Evil event.

Here, people got to create their own super-powered character simply known as The Rookie, as they join Lex Luthor and the Legion of Doom to take down the Crime Syndicate, evil alternate versions of the Justice League, before they can find the Anti-Life Equation.

While the Legion of Doom is ultimately successful in defeating the Crime Syndicate and The Rookie is offered an option to join the Justice League, players can reject the League’s offer and permanently join the Legion to take part in their future criminal activities.

The PS4 era was a bountiful time for new PlayStation hits like Horizon Zero Dawn and Ghost of Tsushima to appear, but it was also a somewhat somber time that saw beloved franchises end. This included the superhero-like Infamous series, which concluded with Infamous Second Son.

Infamous Second Son follows the new protagonist Delsin Rowe as he inadvertently acquires Conduit powers, setting out to save his Akomish tribe and the greater Seattle population from the corrupt Department of Unified Protection.

However, Delsin’s time fighting the DUP can wind up corrupting him, as players can commit several evil Karma actions like corrupting and executing people. This can result in Delsin taking all of the Conduits’ powers, taking control of Seattle, and even destroying his own reservation by the end of the game.

Fans of the original Xbox who want play adventure titles that feature villains as protagonists should check out these 10 games

Arkane Studios’ Dishonored was famous for the sheer number of ways people can play through the game and change the city Dunwall through their actions. Arkane made sure to expand upon this level of player freedom in 2016’s Dishonored 2.

Like Dishonored , players in Dishonored 2 can complete the game without being spotted once or even without killing anyone, but they can also sow high chaos by killing practically everyone they see in the Empire of the Isles.

If players go down this high chaos route as Corvo, the former bodyguard will take the Empire’s throne for himself and become the brutal Emperor Corvo the Black, while a high chaos ending as Empress Emily Kaldwin will end with her ushering a new imperialistic rule and becoming known as Empress Emily the Butcher.

For anyone who played Assassin’s Creed Valhalla, they already knew the endgame of Assassin’s Creed Mirage, but they likely didn’t expect just how devastating the past of the late ninth century Hidden One Basim Ibn Ishaq would be.

Set roughly a decade before Valhalla in Baghdad, Assassin’s Creed Mirage follows the young orphan and thief, Basim, tormented by nightmarish visions of a jinni as he sets out to become a Hidden One after his friend Nehal accidentally killed the Caliph al-Mutawakkil.

While Basim is able to become a Hidden One and assassinates many Baghdad members of the Order of the Ancients, it’s eventually revealed that the jinni and Nehal were the consciousness of the ancient Isu known as Loki, who deceived Basim into killing the Caliph and eventually into giving up control of his own body.

Most of the protagonists of Ubisoft’s Far Cry series are chaotic anti-heroes, not true saviors, but one lead from the series could be considered as a villain due to their actions that lead to the deaths of thousands. That would be the Deputy from Far Cry 5.

Taking place in the western U.S. state of Montana, Far Cry 5 sees the unnamed Deputy travel to Hope County as they attempt to apprehend the cult leader Joseph Seed, and stop his militant followers from taking over the county based on a belief that Seed would save humanity.

However, if players choose to fight the cultists and ultimately arrest Seed, it’ll turn out that Seed was actually right all along as nuclear bombs begin to detonate all over the country, making the deputy responsible for numerous deaths whose lives could have continued on into the apocalypse seen in Far Cry New Dawn.

If you like games that don't force you to be the good guy just because, try these ten FPS games where you're the anti-hero.

The Lord of the Rings universe is inching closer and closer to its 90th anniversary, and over those 90 years, there have been countless adaptations and expansions upon J. R. R. Tolkien fantasy world. One of the worst expansions of his work was undoubtedly The Lord of the Rings: Gollum.

A LOTR game starring only Gollum, The Lord of the Rings: Gollum follows the Stoor Hobbit as he attempts to escape Mordor and searches for the Shire during the events of The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring.

While Gollum does make a few friends during his imprisonment, he doesn’t go out of his way to save them from Orcs and other creatures like the giant spider Shelob, and still vows to eventually make his way to Shire so he can kill Bilbo Baggins and take back the One Ring.

The eighth console generation was an era full of remasters and remakes, with one of the PS4’s best exclusive adventure game remakes being Bluepoint Games’ Shadow of the Colossus.

A complete modern remake of Team Ico’s PS2 masterpiece of the same name, 2018’s Shadow of the Colossus follows the same plot as the original game, with players embodying the young Wander as he sets out to slay 16 massive colossi in an effort to revive a fallen damsel.

As Wander slays each colossi, however, his body begins to slowly deteriorate, up until it’s eventually revealed that the colossi were actual peaceful giants who were keeping the evil entity Dormin at bay. The final colossi’s death frees Dormin to possess Wander’s body.

Unlike The Lord of the Rings: Gollum, one of the better LOTR video games to debut on the PS4 was Middle-earth: Shadow of War, the sequel to Monolith Productions’ Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor.

Set primarily in between The Hobbit and Fellowship, Shadow of War follows the ranger Talion and the Elf spirit Celebrimbor once more, as they forge a new Ring of Power to take over the armies of Mordor, defend Gondor, and ultimately defeat Sauron.

However, all of Talion’s efforts in Shadow of War and Mordor turn out to be in vain, as Celebrimbor plans to abandon Talion and simply replace Sauron to become a new, imperialistic Bright Lord. Talion is forced to become a Nazgul and eventual servant to Sauron to stop Celebrimbor.

JRPGs have a reputation for turning a simple story into one that challenges your viewpoints, and the PS4 era had some of the best.

The PS4 era saw the God of War franchise be completely renewed with the phenomenon that was 2018’s Norse mythology-focused God of War, but before that game debuted, PS4 players were able witness Kratos’ most destructive acts in God of War III Remastered.

Taking place immediately after the events of God of War II, God of War III Remastered sees Kratos and the Titans launch an all-out war against the Greek Gods of Olympus, with Kratos personally slaying most of the Olympians and Titans such as Gaia, Cronos, and his father Zeus.

While Kratos is attempting to avenge his fallen family, Spartan worshippers, and Pandora, his quest for vengeance ultimately dooms most of the world’s population as Poseidon’s death floods the world, Hera’s death kills most plant life, and Hermes’ death unleashes a deadly plague.

One of the better PS4 adventure games that features villains as protagonists is Naughty Dog’s The Last of Us Part II as it features not one but two playable villains: Ellie and series newcomer Abby Anderson.

The Last of Us Part II is largely focused around the fallout of Joel Miller’s decision to stop the Fireflies from experimenting on Ellie in The Last of Us, to find a potential cure for the zombie-like Cordyceps infection, with Abby being the daughter of the doctor who was supposed to experiment on Ellie.

What ensues is a bloody adventure of revenge as Abby and her Fireflies friends murder Joel for killing Abby’s dad, causing Ellie to seek her own revenge by killing all of Abby’s friends, leaving both characters as traumatized, murderous shells of their former selves and villains in the eyes of many survivors.

JRPGs sometimes put you on the other side of the good guy. Here are 8 PS2 JRPGs where you're actually the villain.

#4210. The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin may be your next anime gacha obsession, with a hint of Ghibli, and this latest trailer may be what sells you on it

There's another free-to-play action RPG very much on the horizon. Will this be the one to win you over?

It seems like we’re getting one of these every few months, but the world of mobile action RPGs that look like the games that, just a few years back, were only possible on consoles is expanding with another new entry.

Netmarble, a studio and publisher known for its free-to-play games on mobile and PC, recently unveiled the launch date for The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin, its next major release that’s very much coming for the Genshin Impact crowd.

The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin is an open-world action RPG based on the world of The Seven Deadly Sins anime and manga. The game takes place in the world of Britannia, which looks similar to the way it does in the anime.

That said, the story of the game is not based on the anime or manga, Instead, it’s an original story set in the universe of the show. You play as Prince Tristan of the Kingdom of Liones who must find a way to bring order back to Britannia.

The gameplay should be familiar to anyone who played a free-to-play action RPG in the last decade. It features action combat, a roster of diverse heroes that you assemble to form teams, and a large pretty world to explore where you’ll also get to meet new characters.

Speaking of which, while Origin has its own original story, expect to be teaming up with characters from the series - some of whom wouldn't be able to meet naturally. You can thank the game's multiversal story for that.

Beyond all the serious business of saving the world and battling monsters, The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin also has a cozy, relaxing side. You’ll be able to fish, cook, forage and take on the beauty of the world with your pals.

The game has a bit of an unusual release schedule. It’s set to arrive on PC, PS5, iOS, and Android. PC (Steam), and PS5 players will be able to jump in starting March 16, whereas the global mobile launch is scheduled for one week later, on March 23.

You can pre-register right now on the official website if you’re interested in earning a few rewards when the game launches. You can, of course, always wishlist the game on Steam and the PlayStation Store, too.

#4209. Speedrunners Didn't Take Long To Find New Ways To Break Ocarina Of Time

Ocarina of Time has only been out on Switch 2 for a matter of days, but that has proven more than enough time for the speedrunning community to find a bunch of new exploits in it (thanks for the heads-up, IGN).

Within the first few hours, those who know the N64 game inside and out were hard at work finding ways to cut corners or otherwise break the game to wrap things up as quickly as possible.

Zelda speedrunner gymnast89 managed to hit credits in as little as four and a half hours on the day after the game's launch (we were still marvelling at Kokiri Forest's water effects at that point), and the skip techniques have only multiplied since then.

The biggie at the time of writing is a new glitch that sends Link soaring into the sky, bypassing a bunch of puzzles and looking particularly badass as he does so. Speedrunner ZFG was seemingly the first to discover the move, which relies on some careful positioning around the game's Magic Bean flowers. A series of hops and skips with the camera angle just right, and the game's physics system goes into panic mode, giving Link a real impressive vertical jump.

It doesn't seem to be tied to Shadow Temple skips, either. Other players have found that you can replicate a similar move from the comfort of an empty chest, flitting between Ocarina tracks or using specific items to once again send Link on the up and up.

But what about those sections of the speedrun where Link needs to be on Terra Firma? The remake boasts a brand new dash button for quicker on-foot travel, but there must be an even quicker way, right?

Well, it looks like it! u/Pomps8a took to Reddit with the following strat, which lets Link roll quicker by interrupting the animation with an attack at the end. It's perhaps not the most elegant solution, and there doesn't seem to be any one-to-one matchup at the time of writing to see how much quicker it is, but anything that helps shave off valuable milliseconds is always handy to those in the know.

There's another glitch doing the rounds that lets speedrunners hop over previously inaccessible ledges by item swapping in mid-air. So, if the above big jump is too much, then at least they've got the option of a smaller big jump.

And for those wondering, no, all of this manipulation doesn't work wonders for Link's physical well-being. Skipping big chunks of the game means that a bunch of the remake's new cutscenes are thrown off whack — with Child Link appearing in Adult Link clips, and vice versa — and the Hero of Time looks all the worse for it.

Just look at the poor boy in the following post-sequence break screens from ZFG's recent speedrunning stream:

Honestly, we've been laughing at the above 'Lonk' and 'Lunk' for longer than we care to admit. Look at his little face!

We knew it wouldn't take long for the speedrunning community to find ways to break the remake, but we'll admit that this many glitches so early is rather impressive. We're sure that even more will be unearthed in the coming days/months/years.

Even without all of the glitches, Ocarina of Time is still a damn good time on Switch 2. We awarded the game a 9/10 in our review, calling it "unquestionably the best way to play one of the most seminal games of all time".

#4207. Marathon may actually have a shot as Server Slam hits it big on Steam

Marathon's latest public open weekend has kicked off, and it looks like enough people have showed up to play it.

Things are officially looking better for Marathon. The game’s Server Slam, essentially an open beta that’s freely available everywhere, has kicked off. This is the last chance for anyone curious about Bungie’s next big game to play it before it officially goes on sale next week.

Considering how unpopular the game has been throughout its development, and judging by the feedback from earlier closed beta tests, the turnout for the Server Slam is definitely encouraging.

The Marathon Server Slam has been online for a little over 12 hours on Steam, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S. Only one of those platforms shares player numbers, of course, but it's enough to offer some visibility into how popular the test has been.

Immediately after servers went live, Marathon shot up the Steam most played charts. The game quickly achieved a peak of 143,621 concurrent players (via SteamDB), which is very respectable. Given that the Server Slam will be available for the entire weekend, there’s every chance the numbers will go up.

These figures are particularly encouraging when you look at Arc Raiders, the current top dog in the extraction shooter space, and the game that stole Marathon’s thunder last year when the two of them were being promoted by their publishers. Marathon, of course, got delayed out of 2025, which allowed Arc Raiders to launch first. It, of course, ended up proving that extraction shooters can be mainstream hits.

Like Marathon, Arc Raiders hosted its own server slam just a few days before its launch. That open test attracted 189,668 concurrent players at its peak, which is not that far off from Marathon’s so far.

Assuming positive word of mouth continues, more players are bound to jump in over the weekend and perhaps get Marathon to match or even exceed Arc Raiders’ record. At any rate, this is good news for beleaguered Bungie and points to what could be a big launch.

Marathon arrives March 5 on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S.

#4206. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (2026) Review - Exceptionally Familiar

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo 64 is the most important video game ever made… to me. My byline would not appear in the pages of Game Informer without my original experience playing that game. But it is nearly 30 years old, and despite establishing many important staples of 3D gaming, its age is becoming more apparent. Ocarina of Time was due for a re-examination, and its remake is a wonderful recreation of the 1998 experience with improvements on basically every element: visuals, storytelling, timeless design, and more. It is, however, a remake, and the coloring (though expertly done) is firmly inside the lines.

Ocarina of Time is gorgeous. That the game is less than 25 GB is an engineering marvel. I never quite came around to the odd looks of child Link or Zelda, but every other character, environment, enemy, item, and boss looks incredible. I eagerly looked forward to meeting every weirdo in Hyrule to see their new look, and was never disappointed. The ReDeads and Stalchildren are more traumatic than ever, and every NPC childhood crush I thought I had moved on from was reignited. Watching the sun rise and set over Hyrule feels as magical as it did in the past.

The same accolades can be awarded to the soundtrack. The new orchestrations are incredible, and watching Link’s 4K fingers play the proper notes on his ocarina is mesmerizing. Nintendo continues to fumble voice acting with stiff performances, but thankfully the vast majority of dialogue – one of the primary changes in this remake – is not spoken. Characters don’t necessarily have more to say, but what they say is more impactful, and there are a handful of small but exciting expansions to character and story details. Nothing is groundbreaking or changes how you look at familiar elements, but it manages to be simultaneously nostalgic and improved.

And that’s the closest I got to what I would debatably call a problem: It all looks new, but doesn’t feel particularly new. Ocarina’s overall design holds up. The time travel element is surprising and creates great opportunities to see the world change and evolve; puzzles and their solutions are rewarding; the basics of combat, though simple, are thrilling. All those elements have been adjusted, but not overhauled. Dungeons and their puzzles have been tweaked to remove annoyances (such as fewer keys in the Water Temple), and the new swordplay effects make connecting your blade to monsters feel incredible. But they’re all ultimately small changes that don’t cast Ocarina in a new light or consider its history. It’s a straightforward recreation. But an admittedly very good one.

The biggest, most impactful changes are the new full camera control and active jumping. Swinging the camera around to take a closer look at the upgraded environments is genuinely stirring, especially in the locations that used to be pre-rendered. There is an undefined and exclusive-to-video games emotion I experienced often while trekking locations I thought I knew so well, only to realize I have never seen or looked at it in this way, and I chased and captured that feeling all over Hyrule. Jumping may seem small, but it made me a more active participant in exploration. It also has the benefit of making some encounters feel somewhat trivial (turns out being able to jump over Blade Traps really diminishes their threat), and I was just fine with that.

The beautiful 2026 version of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time does not study the legacy or impact of the landmark game on the video game medium. Instead, it is a meticulous and incredibly impressive recreation of one of the best games ever made. I was rarely surprised during my playthrough, but I was incredibly excited to see old friends and I happily share without embarrassment that playing through its final hour made me cry. For many like me, the original Ocarina of Time is an impactful adventure that arrived at a time in their lives when magic still felt real. Playing the game again 28 years later and appreciating the care taken to maintain and improve that original vision was the ultimate surprise of the whole experience: I didn’t expect to be so moved.

Alex Van Aken contributed to this article.

#4205. Exterminauts Preview: A Second Shift On Planet Tian Proves The Loop Works

My second shift on planet Tian came with a new account and no shortcuts. Exterminauts’ loop still delivered, solo or with friends at your back.

The last time I played Exterminauts, I was setting my editor-in-chief and one of the game’s developers on fire at gamescom. That was a curated session alongside people who knew exactly what they were doing, and it was glorious chaos from start to finish. This time, I started the way most players will when the game launches: on a brand-new account, with nothing unlocked and nobody from the studio at my shoulder.

Weaponized power tools, alien pest control, and the most friendly fire I've committed in a single session. Exterminauts is already feeling special.

Full disclosure: the Exterminauts team very kindly gave me beta access and a key, and answered some of our questions, too. I’ve played around six hours, which isn’t nearly as much as I would have liked, so I haven’t seen the deep end of the build system or the toughest contracts. What I did get was a proper look at the first few days on the job, and those days were very good.

The biggest difference for me from gamescom is the tutorial, and it’s a genuinely good introduction that gives new players a proper footing before planet Tian starts throwing things at them. From there, the game is fully committed to the bit. You start and end each mission at the same point, so every run feels like a shift: clock in, head out, deal with whatever the planet has in store, and come back to get paid. That paycheque goes back into your work gear and sponsorships.

Promotions follow the same logic. Each rank asks something different of you, from simply completing two jobs early on to finishing three of the extra tasks that pop up mid-job, or unlocking a new specification. Every promotion brings more dangerous work with it, and you can feel yourself genuinely getting better at your job. You’re not a chosen one, you’re a field worker who earned the next rung on the ladder.

If anything, the game sometimes leans a little too hard into that fantasy. At times, the whole thing has a very “we’re the lads, and we’re getting the job done” energy, that sometimes has the opposite effect of taking me out of the setting because it feels forced. Still, it does feel like Exterminauts knows very specifically who it’s trying to win over.

The jobs themselves have some nice touches. Every so often, you’ll need to weld something back together, and the game rates your accuracy while gently guiding your aim. Other tasks, like hauling a fuel tank while a teammate waits at a terminal to relaunch a device, are designed to split the work. In practice, nobody stands still at a computer while their friend gets swarmed, so it mostly turns into everyone protecting everyone.

Our preview of Turok: Origins explores the class structures, the multiplayer dynamics, and the feeling of Saber Interactive's upcoming 2026 title.

The extra jobs that pop up mid-run are the best of the bunch, because they stop you sprinting from objective to objective and pull you into corners of the map you’d otherwise never see. Some are modest, like having to kill some monsters after activating a mysterious looking device, to get rewarded with additional max health for the run. Others are much bigger, like stumbling across an abandoned mech that only one person can pilot until its ammo runs dry. It’s a lovely way of rewarding curiosity.

From there, the game is fully committed to the bit. You start and end each mission at the same point, so every run feels like a shift: clock in, head out, deal with whatever the planet has in store, and come back to get paid.

All that wandering means meeting a lot of wildlife, and the enemy variety stood out to me immediately. My favourite is the Hot Potato, a little fire monster that attacks you by rolling into you, and I can’t explain why, but the name just does it for me. It’s in wonderfully strange company, from pests that are mostly mouth and launch themselves at you, to long-necked ones firing lasers from a single giant eye, to floating balloon-like creatures that release swarms of flyers to shock you. And the planet they all call home is still a big wow, with a colour palette so dynamic that even rolling fire potatoes look lovely.

My primary weapon was, well, just a gun. What I’ll remember is the reloading: the magazines are small, which makes sense when you’ve only just started the job, but when a tide of pests rolls in and you just want to clear it and move on, constant reloads get frustrating fast. Your weapons will get stronger, but so will the enemies, and I do wonder whether they’ll still feel a little spongy for the size of your magazine.

The special weapons are a different story. I mostly used the plasma sludge launcher, which coats enemies in corrosive gunk that keeps eating away at them, and it’s brilliant against groups and huge enemies alike – though for the really big ones, grenades usually did the job faster. The Overdrive boost makes your special fire quicker and hit harder at the cost of some battery power, and watching an entire pack melt, ringleader included, is one of the best feelings in the game. I didn’t get to try it, but the CrossCut fires comically oversized saw blades that latch onto enemies and keep spinning, and charging a shot keeps them going for longer.

A review of Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 and why it doesn't match up to the original.

Those weapons come from sponsorships, which work a little like classes, each with its own passive. I went with Bullet Crown, which boosts critical hit damage and gives you a rapid-fire SMG, because mostly playing solo, Vardhan’s shared healing didn’t make much sense. I’ll admit I was a little sad about it, though. The Vardhan gear is pink, and I would have looked very cute.

Solo play didn’t feel worse at all, which I didn’t expect. The difficulty seems to scale down appropriately when you’re alone, and it encourages a slower, more methodical style, so I spent a lot of time scoping out high ground and picking enemies off before they got close. Even on missions where perching up high wasn’t an option, it was still a blast. Difficulty runs across eight levels, adding tougher pests, extra repairs and hazards like extreme weather as you climb, but as a new hire, I didn’t get anywhere near the top.

And the planet they all call home is still a big wow, with a colour palette so dynamic that even rolling fire potatoes look lovely.

My other gripe is the extraction phase, which takes so long. Before you can leave, you have to hold off enemies while earning rewards based on your performance against your own party. Solo, when you just want a few quick runs, it drags, even with support items like sentry turrets and a device that gives you a short burst of unlimited ammo. In a group, though, being scored against your teammates is practically an invitation to friendly fire, and having already incinerated a developer, I have no qualms about doing it again.

That’s really where Exterminauts shines. I share the developers’ view that it’s best with a small group of friends, all yelling at each other while the battlefield falls apart around you. The chaos I loved at gamescom is still there; it just needs a crew to get going.

Six hours in, there’s still a real sense of discovery. The builds already look varied, the pests keep surprising me, and the loop keeps pulling me back for one more shift. There’s plenty to work towards, too, from gear upgrades and trinkets with extra passives to a season pass you can either grind through or pay to unlock. If you enjoy the tutorial and the core loop, I think the rest – the feel, the controls, that gorgeous planet – will win you over.

The bigger challenge is everything around it. There are a lot of games like this out there, and Exterminauts will have to work hard to pull people away from their current favourite. At gamescom, the team outlined six-week seasons with no progression resets, and that cadence will need to give players a reason to stay.

For now, the job is a good one. Whether it turns into a career is up to the seasons that follow.

#4204. The Sims 4 is getting paid mods, and a new in-game currency to pay for them

The Sims 4 is about to launch a couple of major initiatives that may not exactly be what players have been looking for.

The Sims 4 has officially entered into its paid mods era. Developer Maxis announced The Sims Maker Program, and The Sims 4 Marketplace - two new destinations to publish, and discover new add-on content.

The two new features will arrive first on PC and Mac, starting March 17. PlayStation and Xbox players will receive them over the next couple of months, which is very much in line with how other franchises have rolled out their own paid mods systems.

The Maker Program is a way for community creators to get their work out there, and profit from it. The content they create will end up on the Marketplace, where other players can browse it, and pay for it if they want to use it in their game.

Created content will be available across all platforms. All previous packs The Sims 4 players should be familiar with will move to the Marketplace, too: once the feature launches, this is where you’re going to find Expansion Packs, Game Packs, Stuff Packs, Kits, and other official additions created by Maxis.

Alongside this, the game is also introducing a new virtual currency - Moola - which is what you’re going to use to purchase Maker Packs, as well as Sims 4 Kits in the Marketplace. A portion of your purchase will go to the creator (roughly 30%) of what you buy.

It is worth noting, however, that you’ll still be able to buy Expansion Packs, Game Packs, and Stuff Packs without having to purchase Moola, or go through the Marketplace. Kits are the only items that will no longer be available on the existing PC/console storefronts. Moola comes in the usual denominations you’ve seen a hundred items in other games’ in-game shops.

In order to start creating custom content and publishing it on the Marketplace, you’ll need to first be accepted into the program. Once that’s done, you’ll be able to directly publish your content on the Marketplace.

In the blog post announcing the new features, Maxis said that creators will have control over the price of their content, and how it's packaged. These are referred to as Maker Packs, which can include Create-a-Sim or Build/Buy items.

You can apply to become a Maker from March 5. Once accepted, you’ll also get access to the Maker Suite, which is what you’re going to use to test your work to ensure it runs smoothly on the different platforms, and eventually publish it.

#4203. Pokémon Pokopia Expansion Pass Part 2: Dazzling Decorations Arrives Next Month With New Accessories And More

The Pokémon Company has revealed that part 2 of the Pokémon Pokopia Expansion Pass, Dazzling Decorations, will go live on Nintendo Switch 2 next month. More specifically, the Dazzling Decorations expansion will launch on December 9, bringing all kinds of accessories to dress up your Ditto and match other Pokémon.

To play the Dazzling Decorations DLC, your version of Pokémon Pokopia must be running the free 3.0.0 software update, and you must have completed the important requests, "Raise the environment level!" and "Rebuild the Pokémon Center!" in Withered Wasteland. You must also have completed Drifloon's request, "Find a doll!"

"Look your best by wearing accessories with your Pokémon friends," the expansion's details read. "Meet new friends and add some flair to your surroundings with new furniture and more Pokémon. No new town will be introduced in Part 2."

Dazzling Decorations follows the Bubbly Basin expansion, which went live over the Summer, and precedes the unannounced Part 3 of the Expansion Pass, set to go live sometime in 2027. The Pokémon Company says Part 3 will bring a new town to explore and rebuild to Pokémon Pokopia.

#4202. Review: Queen's Domain (Switch 2) - An Incredible Tribute To FromSoft, And One Of 2026's Best Surprises

We heard you liked King's Field, now get ready for...

Way back in the mid-'90s, a business software developer called FromSoftware decided to take a crack at making video games and produced a first-person action fantasy game called King’s Field for the original PlayStation. It did well enough to warrant some sequels, and the studio eventually decided to produce a sort of spiritual successor called Demon’s Souls, a major contributor in solidifying what would come to be known as the Soulslike genre.

There are still lots of fans of that original King’s Field gameplay loop that pine for a return to the roots, and while FromSoft has now moved on to bigger things, the indie scene has stepped up in a major way to deliver us a proper successor. Freshly Baked Games' Queen's Domain is a retro-fantasy action RPG that masterfully blends tough combat, addictive exploration, and a thrilling sense of mystery to make this a serious contender for the sleeper hit of the year.

The narrative is set in the Kingdom of Bamaen, a once-peaceful place on the brink of destruction after the resurrection of the evil witch Queen Siraatsu. In an attempt to put an end to the calamity, King Abraon and a group of his strongest warriors sailed to the Isle of Neasied to slay the waking queen before she could regain her full strength, but they never returned and the growing onslaught of monsters seems to indicate they failed. You then take on the role of Prince Berium, who shipwrecks upon the isle and sets out in the hopes of uncovering what happened to his father and putting an end to the threat.

After the initial premise is set up, storytelling then takes a backseat and becomes more of a set dressing that you happen to encounter every now and then. Item descriptions and environmental storytelling help to fill in gaps and give more context, but there are precious few moments where cutscenes or major plot beats play out. This approach works well for the kind of atmosphere that Queen’s Domain has in spades—there’s a menacing, haunting aura hanging over the world as you plumb further into its depths, a lot of which comes from the fear of the unknown.

Gameplay could be most closely described as a slower, first-person Soulslike, tasking you with exploring an interconnected, mazelike world riddled with enemies ready to gank you at every turn. You’ll die a lot, but you’ll also learn a lot along the way, and that learning paired with the incremental upgrades that come with combat and exploration leads to a remarkably satisfying ascending power curve.

Queen’s Domain is the kind of game that feels a lot more intimidating up front than it turns out to be and, as with FromSoft's work, it’s that gradual conquest and mastery of its deeper secrets and mechanics that makes it such an excellent and enjoyable experience.

Combat involves a very methodical pace that prioritises careful, strategic moves during the many tense encounters. Especially at first, a few hits can be enough to put you right at death's door, and healing resources are scarce enough that you'll be stuck with most injuries until you make it to the next shrine. The stakes are pretty high, too, given that death has a terrible finality to it. There are no corpse runs here to offer a chance at redemption—if you die, the game simply sends you back to the last time that you saved and erases all progress since.

You can't just hack 'n' slash your way through hordes of foes, and getting jumped by just three at once can sometimes feel like a notable challenge. When hitting back, a small stamina bar represents your total damage output, and taking a swing empties it completely. You then either have to wait for it to refill if you want another full power attack, or you can get in another shot earlier with proportionately weaker strength.

If you want to double down, you can also hold the attack button to ready a charge move that will do increased damage, but this makes the wait even longer and locks you out of other movement and attack options as you helplessly sit there with your weapon raised.

It may sound frustrating, but this leads to richly rewarding combat encounters once you figure out the nuances of your kit. Every weapon has a different range and its own little quirks to get used to. An early favourite of mine was a short-range torch that can be used to rapidly deal passive fire damage and has a limited-use ranged attack that lets you toss a fireball. The more you use a weapon, the more you’ll level it up and increase its damage output, and some weapons evolve into something more advanced if you use them enough.

You’re constantly finding new additions to your kit that fill in interesting niches, and while you can only carry a few of them on you as active weapons, you’re usually pushed to change up your loadout as you move into new areas and come across new enemy types with different weaknesses and damage type resistances.

This gives you lots of opportunities to familiarise yourself with each weapon’s nuances, building lots of muscle memory and mechanical knowledge alongside the raw stat bumps that make enemies drop faster with each increase.

Despite how central combat is to the loop, it feels like you spend even more time simply exploring the world and trying to tease out the correct path forward. Exploration captures that same sense of awe that some of the early Zelda games instilled, as you find yourself cautiously crawling through a dungeon looking for a key to a door you found or trying to figure out what that switch you just triggered unlocked. There’s no map and few signposts pointing you in the right direction, so a lot of your knowledge of a space comes from stumbling around a new area and trying things.

I was pleasantly surprised to find some Metroidvania elements present to add rewards that keep exploration from getting dull. New abilities, such as an air dash or a throwable knife, give you access to previously gated areas, and you’ll sometimes stumble across a consumable item that permanently boosts one of your stats. This goes a long way in keeping a strong and satisfying sense of forward progression, as you can hardly travel in any direction without finding some upgrade or a new route.

Worth a special mention is just how well Freshly Baked Games champions the themes of wonder and mystery throughout its journey. If you're looking at a distant ledge and wondering if you can get there, the odds are pretty good that you not only can, but there's some sort of treat waiting for you. Sometimes you'll stumble down an obscure side path expecting some minimal pickup, only to suddenly enter an entirely new biome that'll take hours to explore.

The thrill and delight that comes with that constant sense of discovery is something that many modern action games struggle to replicate, and — as much as you can — I would encourage you to go into Queen’s Domain blind and experience everything organically. The magic is somewhat lost if you know where to go and what to do to move forward efficiently, and allowing yourself to struggle with frustrations and overcome them by poking around will be immensely more rewarding.

The graphics are strongly inspired by the blocky aesthetics of the PS1, marked by simplistic environments, chunky models, and unfiltered textures that collectively transcend their lo-fi quality to make for a memorable and fitting art style.

And despite the horror themes present in much of the monster and level designs, there’s a fitting amount of levity to be found in occasional goofiness, such as an unlockable duck-themed shop you gain access to after an early boss encounter. Simple though they may be, the visuals help a lot with immersion, as your imagination fills in the gaps and connects you that much more closely with a given sequence.

The only drawback here is mild performance problems—not present enough to negatively affect the moment-to-moment gameplay, but just enough to be noticeable. In areas with more open space or when you’re being assailed by several foes at once, the frame rate will dip for a few seconds before it catches back up. Sometimes distant enemies will also animate at a much lower frame rate to save on some resources, which can make them appear jittery and unnatural.

I wouldn’t say that these performance issues are significant enough to majorly impact your enjoyment, but they are nonetheless disappointing given the rather simplistic visuals.

Despite the often heavy and dark visual themes, the soundtrack usually leans into a more atmospheric style that bizarrely reminded me of Donkey Kong Country and Metroid Prime. Not only does this often contribute to the grand feeling that comes with discovering a new temple or biome, but it gives a slightly positive feeling as you march onward and overcome new challenges. It’s a surprising soundtrack, but it fits very well.

Queen's Domain is one of the best surprises of the year, coming out of nowhere and asserting itself as one of the most satisfying action-adventure games in recent memory.

The rewarding character progression, challenging combat, lo-fi visuals, and thrilling sense of mystery all combine to make this one an easy recommendation to anyone looking for that old-school FromSoft style that recaptures the magic of playing older Zeldas and doesn't hold your hand. It’ll likely win you over if you give it a fair shot.

I think part of the underlying issue is that a lot of developers want to have it both ways. Which is to say, they want to build largely linear games that largely only reward linear play. . . but they also still want to stick the occasional thing off the beaten track. Which is exactly the wrong design choice to make, because that's roulette logic and leads to obsessively checking every spot even when there's rarely a reward- thus frustration and boredom.

Basically, they actually do need to make a choice, if they want to achieve good game design. Either you build for a iinear game, and need to consistently not reward going off the beaten track ( or not allow such diversion at all ); or you build for an exploratory game and need to consistently reward going off the track.

#4201. Our first look at Diablo 4's Warlock and the game's next season arrive in today's livestream - watch it here

Diablo 4's latest Developer Update is nearly upon us, and it's one plenty of the game's fans and players have been looking forward to.

Diablo 4’s next, long-awaited Developer Update finally airs today. This meaty livestream was first announced nearly a month ago, when Blizzard initially revealed that the game’s next class is the Warlock.

The Warlock’s initial unveiling, however, was incredibly brief, showing no gameplay. It also didn't explain how the class is going to fit within the existing roster. This all changes today.

Blizzard is bringing back its Developer Update livestream programme, which is the more structured, information-dense series of developer showcases. The focus of this one, of course, is going to mainly be on the Warlock class.

The Warlock is one of two classes coming to Diablo 4 with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion. The first, the Paladin, is already available in the game for anyone who pre-orders the expansion. The Warlock will instead arrive alongside the expansion on April 28.

The Developer Update will also include a first look at the game’s next season (Season 12), currently set for March 10. This mini season will only last until the expansion’s release, so it’s going to be interesting to see what it brings to the game.

You’ll be able to watch the showcase live at 11am PT, 2pm ET, 7pm GMT on Diablo 4’s official YouTube, Twitch, and Twitter channels. We’ve embedded the YouTube and Twitch players below for your convenience.

Among the topics the Developer Update will cover are the Killstreaks system, as well as Bloodstained items. As always, you can also expect a Q&A segment at the end of the show, and I imagine there’s going to be a few about the Warlock.

#4199. God Of War Laufey Delayed To May

PlayStation first-party developer Santa Monica Studio has delayed its upcoming action game, God of War Laufey, to May. More specifically, the PlayStation 5-exclusive title will now launch on May 20, representing a roughly three-month delay from the original February 16 release date.

"Since the reveal of God of War Laufey in June, we've been deeply grateful to see so much excitement for Faye's journey through the Everywhen," a statement from the studio reads. "We don't take for granted the trusted place in the studio to make an extraordinary experience worthy of the passion and dedication of our fans. With this in mind, we've made the decision to delay God of War Laufey's release to May 20, 2027. We will make the most of each moment until then by putting in the finishing touches and pushing the game to its fullest potential. On behalf of everyone on the team, we appreciate your patience and we'll be back to share more updates soon."

God of War Laufey stars Faye, Kratos' deceased wife from his Norse adventures, after she ends up in the mysterious realm known as the Everywhen following her death. There, she will fight monsters and creatures from various mythologies alongside a talking gelatinous cube and a talking sword sash. We'll have to wait a bit longer than expected now to see what her adventure entails.

God of War Laufey will now launch on PS5 next year on May 20. In the meantime, check out this newly revealed weapon, then read about how Amazon's God of War TV series has recast Kratos as Dave Bautista.
