#4180. Company of Heroes 3 Announces Mac Version

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

Many outside of the PC gaming sphere view it as a single homogenized entity centered around Windows, and while plenty of users are focused on Microsoft’s OS, others are shafted by certain releases. Whether it’s Linux or Mac, Windows being the central platform means plenty of releases just miss the alternate PC operating systems, leaving them out to dry when they’d love to join.

Wuthering Waves is one of the biggest Gachas on the planet, and they do far better than most at answering player complaints. Let's go over exactly how!

Relic Entertainment has announced in a YouTube video that its military tactics game Company of Heroes 3 is getting an official macOS port in December, with no exact date specified. Apple-bound players will finally get their chance to play the latest title in the prestigious Company of Heroes series.

World War 2 has been a fixture of gaming practically as long as it has existed, and with its prevalence throughout hundreds of titles, new entries have stepped up to showcase theatres of war outside of Eastern Europe. Company of Heroes 3 makes its mark by focusing on the Italian and North African campaigns, two less glamorous theatres of war that have long earned the spotlight.

The macOS version of Company of Heroes 3 is also launching with the major shake-ups of all previous balance and content patches, including the 3.0 overhaul, but it appears all DLC will need to be purchased separately, one of the biggest criticisms of the game’s current Steam release. To celebrate, the game is currently on sale on Steam as well, giving curious players a chance to hop in as the potential player base grows.

Mac players will also be able to nab the standalone Final Stand mode, a survival battle using most of Company of Heroes 3’s systems to simulate an endless onslaught of attackers. The mode itself has also launched to mixed reviews, as players seem rather tired of the DLC practices of the game itself. The macOS version also requiring the DLC feels like a missed opportunity to win back some fans.

Whether it’s Linux or Mac, Windows being the expectation and central platform means plenty of releases just miss the alternate PC operating systems, leaving them out to dry when they’d love to join.

All in all, the port is exactly what it says on the tin, a chance for macOS fans of the franchise to finally jump on the 2023 release, almost 4 years after its initial drop. Anyone still loyal to the series who hasn’t gotten the chance to play it is likely chomping at the bit and can only hope Relic implements a sale when it finally does make the leap over.

Relic Entertainment has been in a bit of a rough spot as of late, after being passed over as the team for the newest Dawn of War title. Dawn of War, the real-time Warhammer 40K tactics series, has long since been Relic’s baby alongside Company of Heroes, and seeing them off the project is a massive shake-up.

For now, running off this port and last year’s Dawn of War 2 remaster, Relic Entertainment is looking for some small wins to get themselves back in the game, something this new macOS port should really help with. Opening their latest titles to fresh faces should lead to a big boost both in revenue and players, something they desperately need as they move onto their next project.

Relic is stacking up an easy win with the upcoming port of Company of Heroes 3, one of their stronger titles. Fans know the DLC song and dance and are far more willing to play ball, but Relic needs newcomers now more than ever.

#4179. Honkai: Star Rail Version 4.1 livestream reveals a pared-back, four-week update as HoYo plays catch-up

Honkai: Star Rail will continue the Planarcadia story arc in Version 4.1, as the Star Rail Fest presents a new twist.

A new Honkai: Star Rail Special Program has concluded, which means some fresh news about the game’s upcoming major update. Version 4.1, unveiled today as Unraveled for Daybreak, is the action RPG’s next moment, kicking off on March 25.

Unraveled for Daybreak is the next chapter in the ongoing story of Planarcadia, with the Astra Express Crew now invited to a fan fest inspired by their own past journeys. The aptly named Star Rail Fest is ostensibly hosted to allow more of the citizens of Arcadia to experience the Trailblaze.

As everyone’s eyes is fixated on the grand Star Rail Fest, the Phantasmoon Games continue to be in full swing, as does the war with the Supplicants. Star Rail Fest is, however, the big focus of this update, in case it wasn't obvious.

The event is made up of three large-scale zones, each themed around past excursions of the Astral Express. You’ll get to explore the Belobog Zone, Xianzhou Luofu Zone, and Penacony Zone. Later on, you’ll also be able to visit Pearluxe Tower, the headquarters of Pearluxe Corp.

Each area will feature its own attractions, such as the balloon figures of Supreme Guardian Cocolia and the Destruction Engine, the duel against the Lord Ravager Phantylia at Scalegorge Waterscape, and the Pearluxe Tower’s Alloy King Pom-Pom model.

The hot new arrival is bumbling noirish detective Ashveil whom we've met in Version 4.0, and who becomes a playable character with this update. Ashveil is a 5-Star Lightning-Type character, on the Path of The Hunt. You’ll be able to pull for him throughout 4.1's runtime, which is slightly reduced at four weeks instead of the usual six, in order to rebalance the schedule after the extra-long Version 3.8.

In combat, Ashveil is capable of increasing Crit Damage of all allies. He can also mark an enemy as Bait, which reduces the Defence of all enemies on the field so long as this tag holds. If Ashveil uses his Skill on the baited target, he will deal extra Damage and regain Skill Points for the team.

Ashveil can bully that baited target even further by launching Hounding Pursuit. If any of his teammates attacks the Bait, he can further deliver a follow-up attack that gradually accumulates Gluttony for as long as he’s in combat. Gluttony can later be consumed to boost follow-up attack damage.

If he lands a kill, Ashveil continues to deal damage to the next enemy he attacks. That buff is transferred if that enemy is killed. Even in map exploration, Ashveil can be deadly, capable of inflicting Stunned upon enemies within a specific range.

Returning characters this patch will be Hyacine in the first half, and Boothill in the second half. Once again, due to the reduced runtime, their banner reruns will be slightly shorter than normal, at just two weeks each instead of three — so be sure to take that into account if you're planning on pulling for either of them.

Version 4.1 also adds the Wispae War Saga, a new activity where you can practice your leadership skills by commanding different types of Wispae Soldiers in the Graphia Academy. You can upgrade each one, use spell cards to alter their effects, and later face other champions. You ultimately want to play this to unlock new Wispae Companions, not to mention complete the challenges within.

Finally, Version 4.1 marks the start of a new Arcadian Chronicles phase in the Divergent Universe. You’ll be able to use Waypoint Pass cards to explore the different areas. HoYo is also bringing back Planar Fissure and Garden of Plenty with double rewards. And as ever, if you log in for at least seven days after downloading the new patch, you’ll earn 10 premium banner pulls.

#4178. Dandori Academy Is The Perfect Addition To Pikmin 4 Switch 2 Edition For Major Pikmin Fans

Pikmin 4's Switch 2 Edition brings some welcome upgrades to the original game, but whether they're worth the cost depends on your love for Pikmin.

While Mario might be the face of Nintendo, there’s no doubt that Pikmin also holds a special place in Shigeru Miyamoto's heart, as evidenced by the recent Pikmin Day Nintendo Direct. Although there is still no word that we’ll be getting Pikmin 5 anytime soon, Pikmin 4 is thankfully getting some new features to help tide players over as part of the Pikmin 4 Nintendo Switch 2 Edition plus Dandori Academy.

Whether you’ve already played the original and are considering the $10 upgrade pack, or never picked it up and are thinking about grabbing the full Switch 2 Edition now, it’s important to know what to expect. Switch 2 Editions aren’t a new idea, as several games have already received the same treatment, but no two have been exactly alike.

Tears of the Kingdom’s Switch 2 Edition reduced load times and introduced compatibility with the Zelda Notes app. Meanwhile, games like Mario Party Jamboree received an entirely new game mode that utilized the Switch 2’s exclusive features. Pikmin 4’s Switch 2 Edition falls somewhere between those two.

Pikmin 4 was already a decent-looking game when it released on the original Switch, so it should come as no surprise that even though it displays in 4K when docked, there’s no truly noticeable difference in visuals between the Switch 2 Edition and just playing the original version on your Switch 2. At least not one significant enough to note.

That said, even though the visuals didn’t need an upgrade, there are a few welcome changes to the gameplay. Alongside the addition of GameShare support for Dandori Battles, the biggest change comes in the primary game mode, more specifically, to Pikmin 4’s adorable alien pup, Oatchi.

Rather than relying solely on your button inputs to command Oatchi, you can now say the command directly into the mic. However, I did have to mess with the feature’s settings a little before I could use it properly.

Default settings don’t filter out background noise, so the sounds of my TV and toddler were causing Oatchi to rush around wildly without a direct command. Then, filtering out too much sound forced me to yell directly into the mic for the command to work. However, once I found the sweet spot for my environment, it became a surprisingly useful feature.

For one thing, Oatchi didn't appear to take time to charge up his Rush when obeying voice commands, so it’s quicker and more convenient, which is great when targeting moving enemies. I ended up using it more than I anticipated, and appreciated that it was optional so I could turn it off when I didn’t want to disturb anyone. It might be a small change, but it’s a fun and welcome one.

Given the minor changes to Pikmin 4’s base game, the addition of Dandori Academy is the main reason to pick up its Switch 2 Edition. Dandori Academy is an additional game mode that can be accessed from the game’s title screen and played without progressing the primary story mode at all. It consists of timed mini-games that test your skills at collecting treasure and delegating tasks to your Pikmin.

You’re free to do practice mini-games as often as you’d like, but every Friday, Saturday, and Sunday there will be an Exam Event. The exams are a way to show how well all your Dandori practice has paid off, especially since you only get one attempt per exam, and you’ll be awarded a medal based on your score. Certain scores can even earn you points towards rewards, including for the Pikmin Bloom mobile app.

You do need an active Nintendo Switch Online membership to share high scores online and access specific rewards, so keep that in mind if you plan to participate in exams.

There are three difficulty levels for the exam – Elementary, Advanced, and Graduate – with two exams per difficulty.

Overall, the Dandori Academy mini-games aren’t that different from everything you do in the main game. That said, the time limit does add some intensity, and I appreciate that there’s no single right way to earn a high score, so you do have to challenge yourself to use different strategies. For example, some players might prioritize collecting treasure at the start, while others focus on increasing their Pikmin count first.

I also found that even Elementary difficulty proved a bit of a challenge, so if you’re worried that things will be too easy, I don’t think that should be a major concern. If you’re like me and find collecting treasure one of the most fun parts of Pikmin, it’s easy to spend hours in practice mode, which also benefits you beyond just improving your skill.

Completing multiple practice sessions earns you Redo Passes, which will allow you to retake an exam if you don't get the score you want. There is a cap on these, so you can’t farm them indefinitely, but it is nice that your hard work earns you a second chance on an exam you might’ve accidentally botched.

Overall, Pikmin 4 Switch 2 Edition improves on everything that was already great about Pikmin 4. It’s still a charming game that offers more hours of fun gameplay than some of Nintendo’s other titles, now with a few extra features to improve the game’s quality of life.

As for whether it’s worth the upgrade or extra cost, I think that comes down to how interested you are in Dandori Academy. Since the exams themselves require you to hop into the game every weekend, and you need Nintendo Switch Online to enjoy the full benefits, I worry that most players might not be all that interested.

All the mini-games are incredibly fun, don’t get me wrong. I just can’t realistically see myself or many others logging in every weekend to participate in exams beyond the first month or two, so I can only recommend this to those who genuinely love Pikmin, utilize the Pikmin Bloom app, or have been looking for a way to ease the wait for the unannounced, but increasingly likely, Pikmin 5.

#4177. Award-Winning Composer And Musician Jon Batiste Talks Ocarina Of Time's Music And Why 'Guile's Theme' Goes With Everything

Jon Batiste has collaborated with the likes of Alicia Keys, Lenny Kravitz, Prince, Stevie Wonder, Willie Nelson, and many more. He performed the national anthem at Super Bowl LIX. He's headed up the musical efforts of The Late Show with Stephen Colbert. He's taken home more awards than we can realistically list in this article (including eight Grammys, as well as an Academy Award, a BAFTA Award, and a Golden Globe). But as I sit down with Batiste for a brief conversation about video game music, his energy transcends the Zoom call.

Before I can even ask a question, Batiste begins singing to greet me, then nerds out about my NBA Jam and Street Fighter II cabinets. He begins humming the menu music from NBA Jam and reminiscing about all the quarters he pumped into his local Street Fighter cabinet. The Louisiana native and Juilliard School alum has been an ardent gaming enthusiast for nearly three decades, with compositions from games like Sonic the Hedgehog and Final Fantasy VII inspiring his earliest musical endeavors. Spend enough time watching video game music performances on social media, and you'll likely soon find videos of Batiste sitting with famed Final Fantasy composer Nobuo Uematsu, or of Batiste performing gaming music.

With The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time delivering some of the most iconic music of all time (and Batiste famously loving the music), it makes sense that Nintendo would bring him out to New York to serve as a special guest at the launch event for the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on Switch 2. I sat down with Batiste for a few minutes to chat about his love of video game music, his history with Nintendo, and why "Guile's Theme" from Street Fighter II just goes so well with everything.

Ocarina of Time is easily one of the most important video games ever made, and one of the things that makes it so special is the music. What about Ocarina of Time sticks out to you sonically?First off, if you want to get super inside baseball, technical music nerdery, which I love to do, in the compositions, there's a way that major chords and minor chords in... no sevenths, just root, third, fifth. They alternate, and it creates this magic that is, like, it's wistful, and it's simple. It feels ancient, and it feels like it's the music that is going on in your mind as you're generating thoughts and your imagination is churning. And the major chords are happening just after the minors in this contrary motion that's happening, so it feels like the music is going like this: It's going up – major, minor – like [sings the main Legend of Zelda theme song].

So, it's expanding and contracting, which is a musical allegory for the expansion and the openness of the world that Link is in. It's like [Koji Kondo] figured out how to capture the essence of the gameplay, but also the essence of magic and simplicity, which I think is really what makes... that's the music's power! So, you could listen to the music in the game, and you could also listen to it apart from the game and experience that magic.

Are there any tracks in Ocarina of Time that stand out to you as the most musically sophisticated or compositionally impressive?Oh man. Well, I think of it as a suite, so that's what makes it actually... there's nothing that's more or less complex, but the thought to figure out how to make all of the themes be interrelated yet singular. "Song of Storms" is, like, for me, that's a personal favorite. That's why I like to play it. I like to play a lot of the themes. That's how I grew up! I would play the game, and then, I would go to an instrument. Once we played for hours on Nintendo, we'd go and play Nintendo on piano! It was like a trade-off there, you know? I've been doing this since I was about 11 years old.

Taking it back to that 11-year-old Jon, talk to me a little bit about your history in general.Okay, so my history with Nintendo goes back to the NES. Christmas morning. Duck Hunt. You remember that? Maybe the first game I ever played. No, the first game I ever played was Donkey Kong, and then Duck Hunt, and then Super Mario Bros. Staples! We're talking about the early '90s. We had a room where I would go – it was my domain – and we had this blue shag carpet, and I would sit back there, and I would basically disappear into the carpet playing Nintendo for hours and hours.

And my mind is kind of... my mind can become a spiral; it can become a tornado. And I realized even then that going into this world of the game, even if I didn't win – it's not about winning or losing – it helps to organize the spiral of my mind and give me ideas and inspiration. So then, I started to get into Street Fighter II when I started to play more communally with my sister and my cousins. Yoko Shimomura, who I also had the pleasure of meeting and collaborating with, she composed incredible themes for each character, and that's when I really started to get a true love for fighting games.

And then, we would play so many of the Street Fighter franchise. We would play a lot of Final Fight. There were so many things... there was Double Dragon, then we got Mega Man... all these different series. Mega Man X is [an] all-time favorite. And then, here comes The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and that sort of expands the canon while also blending all of the elements: score, combat, the sort of linear quality of, like, a Donkey Kong or Super Mario World, and expanding the world in that way, expanding the canon in that way. Mind-blowing! So,  that sort of solidified my palate in terms of my favorite type of game.

You mentioned Street Fighter II. There's a meme about "Guile's Theme" and how it goes with everything. What about that composition makes it so it has the ability to enhance whatever video you pair it with?Wow! So, it has momentum in a way that is extremely [sings the melody of "Guile's Theme"] ... It draws you in, which is what you want [with] anything that you're starting when you're commencing a journey or watching something. You want it to draw you in, and that kind of pulls you in as that call and response. But it's an immediate announcement with the brass, and then the bass call and response. So, it's automatically giving you this feeling that something's happening, and I've got to pay attention to it! So that's the first step right there. And the tempo is really... it's a great tempo! It almost has the feeling of the great themes from, like, an '80s protagonist that's in a fighting movie. I think that was kind of the archetype. Yoko was probably drawing from that archetype, right? The action-hero archetype.

#4176. Zenless Zone Zero Version 2.7 brings Angels of Delusion to the battlefield with playable Nangong Yu

Champions Never Fall to the Past indeed, as Zenless Zone Zero prepares for a major update that fans of Angels of Delusion will appreciate.

HoYoverse has delivered another Special Program for the second day running, this time for Zenless Zone Zero. The developer revealed the full details of Version 2.7, subtitled Champions Never Fall to the Past.

This next major update arrives March 24, adding two new Agents, and introducing the Hollow Champion competition.

Most things in Version 2.7 follow on from the Hollow Champion competition, which brings together old friends and familiar faces, as well interesting newcomers. Everyone is in it to win some big rewards and earn glory.

Among the unexpected participants the competition has attracted are the Public Security's Metropolitan Order Division, and even some former Calydon's Sweepers. A big challenge that awaits is Black Wolf Romeul, who’s capable of increasing his Crit Damage Resistance and Interruption Resistance by activating a Corruptive Barrier.

Romeul can also cause enemies to continuously lose HP, but you can beat him by putting together a squad that can deal sustained Anomaly damage, which will break through the barrier quickly.

Our first new arrival in Version 2.7 is Cissia of the Metropolitan Order Division. She is an S-Rank Electric Attack Agent who automatically gains three stacks of Venom when she enters the battle. Each stack deals Electric Damage while also increasing her Crit Rate for a time.

When she runs out of Venom, which will happen, Cissia can generate more stacks by using her EX Special Attack. She can also use her Basic Attack, Serpent's Kiss, to better utilise the new stacks of Venom she generates.

The other new Agent may be the more exciting. Nangong Yu, the captain and lead dancer of the Angels of Delusion, can now be part of your team. Nangong Yu is an S-Rank Ether Stun Agent who can boost her team’s Anomaly Buildup Rate against Stunned enemies.

Being part of an idol group has its perks, because she automatically regenerates Downbeat as time goes on, and even more any time a squad member inflicts an enemy with Anomaly. Nangong Yu can then use Downbeat - after enough has been accumulated - on charged attacks that keep enemies stunned for longer. Her Ultimate triggers Ether Veil: Delusion Reprise, which boosts the entire squad’s Attack.

Returning Agents in Version 2.7 will be Yidhari, the S-Rank Ice Rupture Agent, as well as Seed, the Electric Attack Agent.

Outside of all the very important action in the core story, this chapter also brings new themed events to Lumina Square’s Simmer Hot Pot Restaurant. The Simulated Battle Trial is also getting some love, with updated mechanics and new enemy line-ups.

#4175. 8 Metroidvanias Where the World Feels Bigger the More You Learn About It

Eric Warner is a Journalist and Multimedia Producer based in New England with over 7 years of experience producing stories for multiple publications

One of the best aspects of video games overall is how they allow people to learn about and explore enthralling worlds in fantasy, sci-fi, or historical settings.

Many gamers would choose to play third-person open-world or narrative-focused adventure titles to explore such worlds, but there are many other game genres that allow people to delve deeper into a world’s environments and lore, such as the backtracking-centered metroidvania.

While most metroidvania games are limited to a 2D side-scrolling-like perspective, many metroidvania games can feel just as large and expansive as those found in RPGs. Especially as players continue to travel through the titles' maps and learn more about their history and inhabitants.

DrinkBox Studios' Guacamelee! is a stylish Mexican folk art and lucha libre-inspired metroidvania that saw players travel throughout the lands of the living and the dead as agave farmer turned luchador Juan Aguacate.

However, DrinkBox strove to go bigger and better with Guacamelee’s sequel, Guacamelee! 2, as that game had Aguacate travel beyond his homeland into the Mexiverse, a multiverse full of wondrous and intriguing alternate timelines.

This game almost immediately made the universe of Guacamelee far larger and more complex than most players would have imagined by just playing the first game, with Guacamelee! 2 allowing Aguacate to meet alternate versions of friends and villains as well as entirely different realms such as El Otromundo.

Konami’s Castlevania franchise is full of titles that allow players to explore and learn more about the supernatural settings and subsequent entries, as they fight vampires and other monsters. One of the more accessible entries for new players would be Castlevania: Lords of Shadow.

A third-person hack and slash metroidvania reboot of the series, Castlevania: Lords of Shadow has players embody the Brotherhood of Light knight Gabriel Belmont in 11th century Europe, as he sets out to defeat the titular Lords of Shadow and Satan himself.

However, Belmont quickly learns that there are far more dark powers hiding throughout the world as, in the Reverie and Resurrection DLCs, he travels to Carmilla's castle to defeat the ancient Forgotten One, only to become Dracula and menace humanity for hundreds of years.

From the best bosses to essential lore explanations, these are eight Metroidvanias that hide their best content behind the most unexpected paths.

Xbox consoles have become homes for many metroidvania titles over the years, with one of the earliest to debut exclusively on a Xbox console in an action-packed way being Chair Entertainment’s Shadow Complex.

Set in the same universe as Orson Scott Card's Empire book series, Shadow Complex is a military sci-fi metroidvania following Jason Fleming as he and his girlfriend, Claire, set out to explore some caves hidden in a mountain.

Things quickly go awry, though, as it’s revealed that the caves were an entrance to a labyrinth-like shadow complex run by the militant Progressive Restoration. Fleming is forced to explore the complex and steal the PR’s gear in order to rescue Clair and stop the PR from inciting a second civil war in the U.S.

One of the better metroidvanias to launch in 2026 was Drop Rate Studio’s Lovecraftian horror game DIVE or DIE - Children of Rain which takes place in the near future after most of the world was flooded by a supernatural, monster-making black rain.

Here, players must manage one of the last human settlements and routinely send people to dive into the leviathan and ruin-filled Abyssal Pool, in search of supplies and ways to appease the Cthulhu-like Rainmaker in 40 days before it destroys the world.

When players initially dive into the Abyssal Pool, they’ll first find the remains of skyscrapers and other buildings. As they continue to dive deeper and deeper below the surface, they’ll find that the Pool has almost no end in sight and is filled with all kinds of unspeakable horrors.

If you're looking for games that subvert your expectations, try these eight Metroidvanias that totally reinvent themselves halfway through.

As mentioned before, Xbox and Microsoft have supported and published many metroidvanias over the years, with some of the best they published undoubtedly being Moon Studios’ Ori and the Blind Forest and its sequel Ori and the Will of the Wisps.

The Blind Forest primarily takes places in the amazing Nibel Forest and its surrounding areas, but the first game teased other lands that were set to be explored in the Will of the Wisps.

Here, the cat-like spirit Ori and the owl Ku find themselves in the Niwen region, which has since suffered from the loss of its own Spirit Tree. This has resulted in Niwen’s inhabitants becoming corrupted and terrorizing each other, showcasing that the world of Ori is full of all kinds of magical forces and creatures.

Of all the Metroid games released over the years, the Metroid Prime subseries is arguably the most popular, with the series notably transitioning its sci-fi gameplay and maneuverability into first-person.

However, if players wanted to explore areas that feel bigger the more people learn about them, then there’s no better entry in the MP series to try out than Metroid Prime 2: Echoes.

Set roughly one year after the first MP, Metroid Prime 2: Echoes sees the bounty hunter Samus Aran travel to the planet Aether to rescue Galactic Federation Marines, only to discover that the planet is home to an advanced moth-like sentient race called the Luminoth and is at the center of a dimensional rift to an alternate hostile world called Dark Aether.

If you're looking for unexplored gems in video games, I recommend these ten Metroidvanias that are unexpected masterpieces.

Some of the more popular metroidvania series may feature vast, enthralling worlds, but sometimes metroidvanias created by small independent studios are those with the largest worlds, with one such game being Valdis Story: Abyssal City.

The second title created by Endlessfluff Games, Valdis Story: Abyssal City follows the fantasy sword-wielding warrior Wyatt and the mage Reina as they set out in search of Wyatt's father only to wind up in the sunken city of Sitheil.

From here, the two young heroes are forced to not only face off against endless waves of angels and demons but also explore and learn more about the seemingly ever-expanding Atlantis-like city of Sitheil, with the game’s ending even suggesting that other magical cities may be hidden throughout the world.

Without a doubt, the best metroidvania to play where the world feels bigger the more you learn about it is Team Cherry’s 2D masterpiece Hollow Knight.

Set primarily in the subterranean insectoid kingdom of Hallownest, Hollow Knight follows an unnamed horned Knight as they set out to explore a world that has since fallen into ruin following an outbreak of a mysterious, violence-inducing infection.

During the Knight’s travels, players will not only be able to interact with numerous insectoid inhabitants and learn more about Hallownest’s past, but also explore several subregions of the kingdom and learn about other far away lands and realms such as the City of Tears, Crystal Peak, and Dream Realm.

Looking for an exciting map to explore in the Metroidvania genre? We have the games with the best maps for you here.
